blocks.title: What ICAI's published papers tell us
bullets: ICAI has not published examiners' comments for Paper 6, so this guidance comes from ICAI's suggested answers, RTPs and MTPs.
76 official items in the period reviewed — 13 past-paper items, 22 RTP items, 41 MTP items. The chapter appears in **every** attempt from May 2024 to May 2026.

Two headings dominate: **Porter's generic strategies** (22 atoms) and **Mendelow's Matrix** (18). Then **core competency** (14 across §3.4 and §3.4.1), **strategic drivers** (7), **channels** (6) and **SWOT** (5).

**ICAI's RTPs print their own chapter headings, and the pattern is exact**: Chapter 1 = questions 7 and 8, Chapter 2 = 9 and 10, **Chapter 3 = 11 and 12**, Chapter 4 = 13 and 14, Chapter 5 = 15 and 16, in all nine RTPs from May 2024 to September 2026. Question 11 is a case; question 12 is a short note.

Four questions repeat almost verbatim across papers: 'How can Mendelow's Matrix be used…' (four papers), 'Write a short note on the key strategic drivers' (six papers), 'the four specific criteria of sustainable competitive advantage' (three papers), 'major core competencies are identified in three areas' (four papers), and 'What are channels? Why is channel analysis important?' (five papers).

blocks.title: How ICAI answers this chapter (study guidance)
bullets: **Generic-strategy cases always follow the same three steps.** ICAI's answer opens 'According to Porter, strategies allow organizations to gain competitive advantage from three different bases: cost leadership, differentiation, and focus', then names the one the facts show, then applies it to the facts. Write that opening sentence every time.

**Mendelow questions want both the process and the quadrants.** ICAI's RTP answer gives four steps — identify stakeholders, assess power and interest, plot on the grid, develop strategies for each quadrant — and its past-paper answer gives the four quadrant names with the management response to each. A full-mark answer carries both.

**'Short note' questions are not short.** ICAI's answer to 'write a short note on the key strategic drivers' runs to a definition plus four numbered drivers with three or four lines each, and closes with an alignment sentence.

Where a case names a **niche or narrow segment plus a premium**, the answer is **focused differentiation** (RTP May 2025 Q11, MTP Mar 2024 S2 Q4(b), RTP Sep 2026 Q13). Where it names **affordability plus premium features together**, the answer is the **best-cost provider strategy** (PYQ Sep 2025 Q5(a), MTP Sep 2026 S2 Q1(c)).

blocks.title: Where candidates lose marks here
bullets: Confusing the **three areas** in which core competencies are identified (competitor differentiation, customer value, application to other markets — Prahalad and Hamel) with the **four criteria** of sustainable competitive advantage (valuable, rare, costly to imitate, non-substitutable). Both are asked, separately, and three times each.

Confusing those four criteria with the **four characteristics** that determine the *sustainability* of competitive advantage (durability, transferability, imitability, appropriability — §3.6.1). Three different four-item lists sit within four pages of each other.

Treating SWOT as purely internal. The study material is explicit that SWOT is **a tool used for both internal and external analysis**, and names its major criticism: it does not generally provide for evaluation in the **competitive context**.

Writing 'focus' when the facts show a narrow segment competing on **price** (focused cost leadership) rather than on **uniqueness** (focused differentiation). ICAI's five-strategy figure distinguishes them.

Forgetting that stakeholders **move between quadrants**: ICAI's own illustration is a GST compliance lapse moving the Indirect Taxes Department from high power / low interest to high power / high interest, and the media from low power / low interest to low power / high interest.

concepts.title: 3.1–3.2 Introduction; Understanding Key Stakeholders
understand: **Introduction (§3.1).** ==Strategic analysis is equally important when it comes to internal environment assessment.== The internal environment is ==**the sum total of people — individuals and groups, stakeholders; processes — input-throughput-output; physical infrastructure — space, equipment and physical conditions of work; administrative apparatus — lines of authority and power, responsibility, accountability; and organizational culture — intangible aspects of working, relationships, philosophy, values, ethics — that shape an organization's identity.**==

==**The internal environment is specific to each organisation.**== It is based on its **structure and business model** and includes all stakeholders like top management, investors, employees and the board of directors. It also involves understanding of the **ethics, principles, work environment, employee friendliness, confidence of investors** and other philosophical and cultural aspects of business, which aim for the success of the organisation.

**Understanding key stakeholders (§3.2).** ==**A firm may be viewed as a coalition of stakeholders — all those individuals and entities that have a stake in its success and can impact it as well.**== They may be employees, shareholders, investors, suppliers, customers, regulators and so on. ==This view of the firm is **in contrast to the earlier view** of the firm, which was considered to be an extension of the owners and shareholders alone.==

==**Stakeholders can be defined as any person or group of individuals, internal or external, that has an interest in, or impact on, the business or corporate strategy of the organisation. They have the power to influence the strategy or performance of that organisation.**==

Generally, stakeholders include **management, employees, shareholders, customers and vendors**. Additionally, **governments, labour unions and local groups** are often considered stakeholders depending on their impact on the particular organisation. ==Each stakeholder or stakeholder group will be **affected by the business strategy** that the organisation chooses and implements.==

**Why identification comes first.** ==Each stakeholder exerts a **different level of influence** and can have **differing levels of interest** in the organisation.== ICAI's illustration: an organisation involved in **healthcare innovation** needs a long-term perspective on its return on investment, because there may be a long time between research timelines and a commercial outcome — while **shareholders, whose main concern is quick profits, may be more hesitant** to support spending on something whose return they may not see in the near future.
==Since the expectations of key stakeholders can influence the organisation's strategy, **a clash of objectives may have unfavourable consequences for the organisation**.==

**ICAI's worked table — key stakeholders of an OTT platform and their requirements.** **Shareholders:** innovation and continuous creative content; total shareholder return (RoI); corporate social responsibility; top rankings of the organisation; highest market share. **CEO and Board of Directors:** prestige; market share; revenue and profit growth; market rankings. **Major vendors (production houses):** growth; stability of ordering; stable margins. **Consumers (viewers):** new content and innovation; better deals and pricing benefits; value for money; continuous supply. **Employees:** wages and benefits; stability of employment; pride of working for a reputed organisation.

Notice what the table teaches: the same organisation owes **five different and partly incompatible things** to five groups. Shareholders want CSR spending and the highest market share at once; vendors want stable margins while consumers want better deals. That incompatibility is the 'clash of objectives' the study material warns about, and it is why the next heading supplies a tool for ranking the groups.
concepts.example: An OTT platform's board approves a ₹500 crore original-content slate. Shareholders read it as innovation (good) and as cash burn delaying returns (bad); production houses read it as stability of ordering (good); viewers read it as new content (good); employees read it as job security (good). All four are stakeholders with a stake in the same decision, and the board cannot satisfy all of them on every dimension — which is exactly why it must first identify which groups hold power and which hold interest.

concepts.title: 3.2.1 Mendelow's Matrix (the Power-Interest Matrix)
understand: ==**The Mendelow Stakeholder matrix (also known as the Stakeholder Analysis matrix and the Power-Interest matrix) is a simple framework to help manage key stakeholders.**==

**Why it is needed.** Managing a project is extremely complicated because it involves **managing the competing interests of various stakeholders**. ==Who needs to know what and when, who needs to give their feedback and who has the final approval can be confusing. **However, managing stakeholders is critical to the success of a project.**== This is where a stakeholder analysis matrix can help.

==**Mendelow suggests that one should analyse stakeholder groups based on Power** (the ability to influence organisation strategy or resources) **and Interest** (how interested they are in the organisation succeeding).==

**The caution the study material adds.** All stakeholders may *seem* to have lots of power, and the organisation may *hope* they would have lots of interest too. But in reality **some stakeholders will hold more power than others, and some will have more interest than others**. ICAI's contrast: ==a **big shareholder** is likely to have high power and high interest; a **big competitor** would have high power to impact strategy but potentially **less interest in the success of a rival organisation**.==

**Developing the grid.** The matrix identifies which stakeholders are incredibly important — the metrics being **High Power and High Interest**, which management would need to **manage closely, while investing a lot of time and resources**. ICAI's example: the **CEO** is likely to have more power to influence the work and also high interest in its success, so **keeping them informed almost daily should be a priority**. By contrast, stakeholders with low power and low interest, **like research institutes seeking an organisation's data**, should be **monitored rarely and minimum effort expended** on them in terms of time and money.
**The four quadrants, in the study material's own words:**

==**KEEP SATISFIED — high power, less interested.** The organisation should put in enough work with these people to keep them satisfied with their intended information **on a regular basis**. Examples: **banks, government, customers**. The grid's instruction: *consult often; increase their interest; can be a hindrance to new ideas or strategic choices.*==

==**KEY PLAYERS — high power, highly interested.** The aim should be to **fully engage** this group, **making the greatest efforts to satisfy them, take their advice, build actions and keep them informed with all information on a regular basis**. Examples: **shareholders, CEO, Board of Directors**. The grid's instruction: *manage closely; involve in decision making; engage regularly and build a strong relationship.*==

==**LOW PRIORITY — low power, less interested.** The organisation should only **monitor** them with no actions to satisfy their expectations; **minimal efforts** should be spent **while keeping an eye to check if their levels of interest or power change**. Examples: **business magazines, media houses**. The grid's instruction: *monitor only, no engagement; general occasional communication.*==

==**KEEP INFORMED — low power, highly interested.** The organisation should **adequately inform** this group and communicate with them **to ensure that no major issues arise**. These audiences can also help with **real-time feedback and areas of improvement**. Examples: **employees, vendors, suppliers, legal experts**. The grid's instruction: *utilise the high interest by engaging in decisions; consult in their areas of expertise and interest.*==

**Movement between quadrants — the point candidates miss.** ==An important thing strategists should be aware of is that **the environment is highly dynamic and certain things might happen that can cause stakeholders to suddenly move between quadrants**.== ICAI's worked illustration: an organisation might inadvertently contravene a regulation, say **GST compliance**, which would cause the regulatory body — the **Indirect Taxes Department** — to move from **High Power, Low Interest to High Power, High Interest**, requiring a different way of managing and communicating with that stakeholder. ==Equally, **media houses would move from Low Power, Low Interest to Low Power, High Interest**. So it is always worth **re-analysing Mendelow's grid in the event of a change in the environment**.==

**The four process steps ICAI publishes for 'how is the matrix used'** (RTP September 2024 and RTP January 2026, identical): **(1) Identify stakeholders** — all individuals, groups or organisations that may be impacted by or have an impact on your activities. **(2) Assess power and interest** — power assessed on **authority, resources and expertise**; interest gauged by **level of involvement, expectations, and potential benefits or risks**. **(3) Plot stakeholders on the grid** — power on one axis, interest on the other, each stakeholder placed by the assessment. **(4) Develop strategies for each quadrant** — fully engage key players and seek their input; keep the high-power/low-interest group satisfied with regular updates so they do not become detractors; keep the low-power/high-interest group adequately informed; monitor the low-priority group.
concepts.example: A hospital chain building a new wing: the municipal corporation holds high power over approvals but little interest in the hospital's success (keep satisfied); the promoter family holds both (key players); the resident welfare association of the neighbouring colony has little power but intense interest (keep informed); a medical journal requesting data has neither (low priority). If the project then breaches a building norm, the corporation's interest jumps and it becomes a key player overnight — the movement ICAI illustrates with the GST example.

expected_questions.question: "The environment is highly dynamic and certain things might happen that can cause stakeholders to suddenly move between quadrants." Explain this statement with the study material's own illustration, and state what the strategist should do about it.
answer_points: Mendelow's Matrix plots stakeholder groups on **Power** (the ability to influence organisation strategy or resources) and **Interest** (how interested they are in the organisation succeeding), producing four quadrants — keep satisfied, key players, keep informed and low priority.
Because the environment is highly dynamic, a stakeholder's power or interest can change, moving it to a different quadrant and requiring **a different way of managing and communicating** with it.

**ICAI's illustration:** an organisation might inadvertently contravene a regulation, say GST compliance. That would cause the regulatory body — the Indirect Taxes Department — to move from **High Power, Low Interest** to **High Power, High Interest**, turning a 'keep satisfied' stakeholder into a 'key player'.
**Equally**, media houses would move from **Low Power, Low Interest** to **Low Power, High Interest** — from 'low priority' to 'keep informed'.

**What the strategist should do:** it is always worth **re-analysing Mendelow's grid for the organisation in the event of a change in the environment**; and even for the low-priority group, minimal effort should be spent **while keeping an eye to check if their levels of interest or power change**.

official_questions.question: How can Mendelow's Matrix be used to analyze and manage the stakeholders effectively?
answer_points: Mendelow's Matrix can be used effectively to analyse and manage stakeholders through a **grid-based approach** by the following steps.

**1. Identify Stakeholders:** begin by identifying all relevant stakeholders for the project or organisation — individuals, groups or organisations that may be impacted by, or have an impact on, your activities.

**2. Assess Power and Interest:** for each stakeholder, assess their **power** to influence the project or organisation and their **level of interest** in its success. Power can be assessed on factors such as **authority, resources and expertise**, while interest can be gauged by their **level of involvement, expectations, and potential benefits or risks**.

**3. Plot Stakeholders on the Grid:** create a grid with power on one axis and interest on the other and plot each stakeholder. High power and high interest go in the **Key Players** quadrant; high power but low interest in **Keep Satisfied**; low power but high interest in **Keep Informed**; low power and low interest in **Low Priority**.

**4. Develop Strategies for each Quadrant:** **Key Players** — fully engage, seek their input and keep them informed; they are crucial to success, so their needs and expectations should be a top priority. **Keep Satisfied** — provide regular updates and address concerns **to prevent them from becoming detractors**. **Keep Informed** — communicate adequately so no major issues arise and use their feedback. **Low Priority** — monitor only, with minimal effort.

ICAI prints the grid itself alongside the steps, with the instructions 'consult often / increase their interest' for keep satisfied, 'manage closely / involve in decision making' for key players, 'monitor only, no engagement' for low priority.
also_asked_as: MTP-M24-S1-SQ4b and MTP-S25-S2-SQ4b ask the identical question with the same published answer; both offer an unrelated OR alternative. RTP-J26-SQ11 applies the same four steps to EcoBuild Constructions' smart city project.

official_questions.question: "Managing stakeholders is critical to the success of a project". Explain how Mendelow's Matrix helps in managing stakeholders and categorizing the stakeholders into groups. (5 Marks)
answer_points: The Mendelow's matrix is a **simple framework to help manage key stakeholders**.

**Managing stakeholders:** Mendelow's Matrix is an essential tool for managing stakeholders effectively in project management, as it involves managing the **competing interests** of various stakeholders. It categorises stakeholders based on their **power and interest** levels, helping project managers identify which stakeholders are incredibly important and **prioritise their engagement strategies**.

**Key Players (High Power, High Interest):** require **close management and regular communication**; engaging them fully ensures their support and input, which is crucial for project success. CEOs and shareholders fall into this category.

**Keep Satisfied (High Power, Low Interest):** they have significant influence but may not be as invested in the project's success; it is essential to keep them satisfied with sufficient information **to prevent potential conflicts**.

**Keep Informed (Low Power, High Interest):** interested in the project but lacking the power to influence its outcome; regular updates and communication **foster goodwill and may provide valuable feedback**.

**Low Priority (Low Power, Low Interest):** require minimal attention; **monitoring their interest and power levels periodically is sufficient**, as they do not significantly impact the project. ICAI closes: the matrix provides a clear framework for categorising stakeholders based on power and interest, facilitating effective stakeholder management and enhancing the likelihood of project success.
official_questions.examiner: No examiners' comments have been published for Paper 6.
also_asked_as: MTP-J26-S1-SQ4b sets the identical statement question with the same published answer, offering the three areas of core competency as the OR alternative.

official_questions.question: Soltex Green Energy is rolling out a major wind project in a coastal town. A local business coalition with strong political ties and deep interest in the project has started influencing policy discussions. The company's strategy team is closely engaging with them while managing other stakeholders differently. What might be the reason Soltex is prioritizing engagement with this specific group? Identify and briefly explain the four types of stakeholder categories businesses typically deal with in such situations.
answer_points: Soltex is prioritising engagement with the local business coalition because they fall under the category of **Key Players** in Mendelow's Stakeholder Matrix. The group possesses **high power** (strong political ties and the ability to influence policy) and **high interest** (deep involvement in the wind project).

As per Mendelow's Matrix, such stakeholders must be **fully engaged, informed regularly, and their advice and expectations carefully considered**, as they can significantly impact the success of the project.
**1. Key Players (High Power, High Interest):** should be closely managed and fully engaged; they are critical to strategic decisions.
**2. Keep Satisfied (High Power, Low Interest):** should be kept satisfied with regular information but **not over-communicated with**.
**3. Keep Informed (Low Power, High Interest):** must be kept adequately informed **to avoid misunderstandings and gain useful feedback**.
**4. Low Priority (Low Power, Low Interest):** require minimal effort, only to be **monitored occasionally**.

official_questions.question: EcoBuild Constructions, a leading infrastructure development company, is planning to launch a large-scale smart city project. The project involves multiple stakeholders, including government bodies, investors, suppliers, local communities and environmental groups — each with varying levels of influence and interest. To ensure smooth project execution and stakeholder cooperation, the management wants to analyze and manage these stakeholders effectively. How can EcoBuild Constructions use Mendelow's Matrix to analyze and manage stakeholders in this project?
answer_points: EcoBuild Constructions can use Mendelow's Matrix through a **structured, grid-based approach**.

**1. Identify Stakeholders:** begin by identifying all relevant stakeholders — government bodies, investors, suppliers, environmental groups and local communities — who may influence or be affected by the project.

**2. Assess Power and Interest:** assess each stakeholder's power to influence the project and level of interest in its success, using authority, resources and expertise for power, and involvement, expectations and potential benefits or risks for interest.
**3. Plot Stakeholders on the Grid:** place each in the Key Players, Keep Satisfied, Keep Informed or Low Priority quadrant.

**4. Develop Strategies for each Quadrant:** fully engage the key players (typically investors and major government approving bodies); keep the high-power, low-interest group satisfied with regular information; keep the high-interest, low-power groups such as local communities and suppliers adequately informed and use their feedback; monitor the rest.

The case is a good illustration of the movement warning: **environmental groups** sit in keep-informed while the project complies, but a single environmental breach would raise their interest and, through regulatory escalation, their power.

official_questions.question: Chic Threads, a boutique fashion brand renowned for its commitment to sustainability and ethical practices, has recently launched a new line of eco-friendly clothing made from recycled materials. The brand recognizes the growing influence of environmentally conscious consumers who actively shape industry standards. (5 Marks)
answer_points: ICAI's published answer places the **environmentally conscious consumers who influence industry standards** in **Mendelow's Matrix**.

Such a group combines **high interest** (they actively shape industry standards and care about sustainable practice) with **power** that grows as their numbers and voice grow — so Chic Threads must engage, not merely monitor, them.

The management response follows the quadrant: **fully engage, take their advice, build actions and keep them informed on a regular basis** if they are treated as key players; **adequately inform and communicate so that no major issues arise, and use their real-time feedback and areas of improvement** if they are treated as keep-informed.

The case is a direct application of the study material's caution that all stakeholders may *seem* to have lots of power: the correct answer depends on assessing power on **authority, resources and expertise**, not on how loudly a group speaks.
It also illustrates movement between quadrants: as environmentally conscious consumers come to 'actively shape industry standards', their power rises and the grid must be re-analysed.

mcqs.question: M/s. ABCD Ltd. is of the considered view that meticulous analysis of its stakeholders will help it build and maintain strong relationships with each group. As an accepted practice, greatest efforts are in place to satisfy Mr. X, the Chief Executive Officer, by taking his advice and keeping him informed with all related information and developments on a regular basis. While preparing a Power Interest matrix of stakeholders, the position of Mr. X will be categorized in which one of the following quadrants?

options.A: Key player
options.B: Keep satisfied
options.C: Keep informed
options.D: Low priority

mcqs.explanation: High power and high interest make a stakeholder a **key player**, to be fully engaged with the greatest efforts to satisfy them, taking their advice and keeping them informed on a regular basis — the study material's own example is the CEO (SM §3.2.1). ICAI key: (A).

why_wrong.B: Keep satisfied is high power but *low* interest — banks, government, customers.
why_wrong.C: Keep informed is high interest but *low* power — employees, vendors, suppliers.
why_wrong.D: Low priority is low on both — business magazines, media houses.

mcqs.trap: The stem's words 'keeping him informed' pull towards 'keep informed'; the quadrant is decided by power and interest, both of which are high for a CEO.

mcqs.question: A leading real estate developer, Green Habitat Constructions, wants to integrate Solar Tech's next-generation panels into its residential and commercial projects. Where would Green Habitat Constructions fall in Mendelow Matrix?

options.A: High power, High interest (Key Players)
options.B: Low power, Low interest (Low Priority)
options.C: Low power, High interest (Keep informed)
options.D: High power, Low interest (Keep Satisfied)

mcqs.explanation: A large developer adopting the product across its projects holds high power (it can make or break volumes) and high interest (its own buildings depend on the panels) — a key player to be managed closely and involved in decision making. ICAI key: (A).

why_wrong.B: Neither low; the partnership is material to both sides.
why_wrong.C: Its purchasing scale gives it real power.
why_wrong.D: Its interest is high, not low — it is integrating the panels into its own projects.

mcqs.trap: Customers are listed under 'keep satisfied' in the study material's examples, but a customer whose own product depends on yours has high interest too.

mcqs.question: A multinational corporation is planning a merger with a local firm in a developing country. The local firm's community has high stakes in maintaining local employment and environmental standards but limited formal authority over the transaction. In Mendelow's terms, this community should be:

options.A: Managed closely as key players and involved in decision making
options.B: Kept informed, with the organisation communicating adequately so that no major issues arise and using their feedback
options.C: Monitored only, with no engagement
options.D: Kept satisfied with regular information to prevent them becoming detractors

mcqs.explanation: High interest with low formal power is the **keep informed** quadrant: adequately inform and communicate to ensure no major issues arise, and use the group for real-time feedback and areas of improvement (SM §3.2.1). ICAI key: (b).

why_wrong.A: Key players need high power as well as high interest.
why_wrong.C: Monitor-only is the low-priority quadrant — low on both.
why_wrong.D: Keep satisfied is for the powerful but uninterested.

mcqs.trap: A community's moral claim feels powerful; Mendelow's power is the ability to influence strategy or resources, assessed on authority, resources and expertise.

mcqs.question: In accordance with Mendelow's Matrix, some stakeholder groups possess high power and high interest in a company's operations. Among the options listed below, which stakeholder group typically falls into that category?

options.A: Business magazines and media houses
options.B: Shareholders, the CEO and the Board of Directors
options.C: Research institutes seeking the organisation's data
options.D: Banks and the government

mcqs.explanation: SM §3.2.1 names shareholders, the CEO and the Board of Directors as the examples of key players — high power, highly interested. ICAI key: (b).

why_wrong.A: The study material's own example of low priority.
why_wrong.C: The study material's own example of low power and low interest.
why_wrong.D: The study material's own example of keep satisfied.

mcqs.trap: Every wrong option is a genuine example from the same paragraph, attached to a different quadrant.

mcqs.question: The rise of environmental NGOs and stricter recycling regulations highlight the importance of stakeholder management. Using Mendelow's Matrix, how should EcoRide position NGOs as stakeholders, and why?

options.A: Low priority, because they are not customers
options.B: Key players, because they hold statutory approval powers
options.C: Keep satisfied, because their interest in the company is low
options.D: Keep informed moving towards key players, because their interest is high and stricter regulation is raising their power

mcqs.explanation: NGOs begin with high interest but limited formal power (keep informed); as regulation tightens, their power rises and they move towards key players — the study material's own point that stakeholders can suddenly move between quadrants. ICAI key: (d).

why_wrong.A: Their interest in the firm's environmental conduct is high.
why_wrong.B: NGOs do not themselves hold statutory approval powers; regulators do.
why_wrong.C: Their interest is high, not low.

mcqs.trap: The static reading (keep informed) is half right; the stem's reference to stricter regulation is the movement cue.

mcqs.question: GEL identified shareholders and the Board of Directors as key stakeholders. Analyze the rationale for classifying them as both high power and high interest.

options.A: They hold formal authority but little concern for day-to-day performance
options.B: They can influence strategy and resources and are directly concerned with the organisation succeeding, so they must be fully engaged, consulted and kept informed regularly
options.C: They are external parties whose interest must merely be monitored
options.D: They have high interest but no ability to influence resources

mcqs.explanation: Power is the ability to influence organisation strategy or resources; interest is how interested they are in the organisation succeeding. Shareholders and the Board score high on both, so the response is full engagement, taking their advice and regular information (SM §3.2.1). ICAI key: (b).

why_wrong.A: That describes keep satisfied.
why_wrong.C: That describes low priority.
why_wrong.D: That describes keep informed.

mcqs.trap: Each distractor is the correct description of a different quadrant.

mcqs.question: According to Mendelow's Matrix, which group of stakeholders requires the highest level of engagement from Titan Tech?

options.A: Employees with high interest but limited influence
options.B: Media houses tracking the industry
options.C: Those with both high power and high interest
options.D: Regulators with high power but low interest

mcqs.explanation: The key players quadrant — high power, high interest — is where the organisation makes 'the greatest efforts to satisfy them, take their advice, build actions and keep them informed with all information on a regular basis' (SM §3.2.1). ICAI key: (c).

why_wrong.A: Keep informed — adequate information, not the highest engagement.
why_wrong.B: Low priority — monitor only.
why_wrong.D: Keep satisfied — enough work to keep them satisfied.

mcqs.trap: 'Highest level of engagement' maps to the quadrant, not to the most numerous group.

mcqs.question: How did Athena Corporation effectively utilize Mendelow's Matrix to manage stakeholders based on their power and interest, ensuring long-term stability and success?

options.A: By treating every stakeholder group identically to avoid accusations of favouritism
options.B: By ranking stakeholders only on the size of their financial stake
options.C: By assessing each group's power and interest, plotting them on the grid, and developing a distinct engagement strategy for each quadrant
options.D: By engaging only those stakeholders who approached the company first

mcqs.explanation: That is the published four-step use of the matrix: identify stakeholders, assess power and interest, plot on the grid, develop strategies for each quadrant. ICAI key: (c).

why_wrong.A: Uniform treatment defeats the purpose; the matrix exists because effort must be differentiated.
why_wrong.B: Financial stake is not the axis; power and interest are.
why_wrong.D: Stakeholder identification is proactive, covering all who impact or are impacted.

mcqs.trap: Option A sounds fair-minded but contradicts the matrix's entire rationale.

mcqs.question: A group of environmental activists consistently raises concerns about a company's environmental impact. While their opinions attract public attention, they hold no formal authority over the company's decisions. How should the company treat this group?

options.A: Keep informed — communicate adequately so that no major issues arise, and use their feedback on areas of improvement
options.B: Key players — involve them in every decision
options.C: Low priority — monitor only, with no engagement
options.D: Keep satisfied — give them enough information to stop them interfering

mcqs.explanation: High interest with low formal power is the keep-informed quadrant, where the study material says to adequately inform and communicate to ensure no major issues arise, and notes that such audiences can help with real-time feedback and areas of improvement. ICAI key: (a).

why_wrong.B: Key players need power as well as interest.
why_wrong.C: Monitor-only would ignore a group with high interest and public attention.
why_wrong.D: Keep satisfied is for the powerful but uninterested.

mcqs.trap: Public attention is not the same as power to influence strategy or resources.

mcqs.question: Based on Mendelow's Matrix, how would you categorize Dealers in the case of Nav-Uday, who have significant influence and expect alignment with the company's future strategy?

options.A: Low priority
options.B: Keep informed
options.C: Keep satisfied
options.D: Key players

mcqs.explanation: Significant influence is power; expecting alignment with future strategy is interest. High on both makes the dealers key players, to be managed closely and involved in decision making. ICAI key: (d).

why_wrong.A: They are low on neither dimension.
why_wrong.B: They have real influence, so not low power.
why_wrong.C: Their interest in the strategy is explicitly high.

mcqs.trap: Dealers are intermediaries and feel peripheral, but for a vehicle maker their influence over volumes is decisive.

mcqs.question: The study material's grid gives the instruction "Consult often; increase their interest; can be a hindrance to new ideas or strategic choices." Which quadrant is this?

options.A: Keep satisfied
options.B: Keep informed
options.C: Key players
options.D: Low priority

mcqs.explanation: SM §3.2.1 grid: keep satisfied (high power, low interest) carries 'consult often, increase their interest, can be hindrance to new ideas or strategic choices'. Key players carry 'manage closely, involve in decision making'; low priority 'monitor only, no engagement'; keep informed 'utilise the high interest by engaging in decisions'.

why_wrong.B: Keep informed is 'utilise the high interest by engaging in decisions; consult in their areas of expertise'.
why_wrong.C: Key players are 'manage closely; involve in decision making; engage regularly'.
why_wrong.D: Low priority is 'monitor only, no engagement; general occasional communication'.

mcqs.trap: 'Consult often' appears in two quadrants' instructions in different forms; the 'hindrance to new ideas' clause is unique to keep satisfied.

mcqs.question: As per ICAI's published answer, a stakeholder's **power** is assessed on the basis of:

options.A: Shareholding percentage alone
options.B: Public visibility and media coverage
options.C: Authority, resources and expertise
options.D: Level of involvement, expectations, and potential benefits or risks

mcqs.explanation: Power is assessed on authority, resources and expertise; interest is gauged by level of involvement, expectations, and potential benefits or risks (RTP Sep 2024 Q12 and RTP Jan 2026 Q11).

why_wrong.A: Too narrow — expertise alone can confer power.
why_wrong.B: Visibility is not one of the three stated bases.
why_wrong.D: That is the published basis for assessing **interest**, not power.

mcqs.trap: Option D is the right list attached to the wrong axis.

recap: Mendelow = Stakeholder Analysis matrix = Power-Interest matrix: a simple framework to manage key stakeholders.
Power = ability to influence strategy or resources (authority, resources, expertise). Interest = how interested they are in the organisation succeeding (involvement, expectations, benefits or risks).

Four quadrants: keep satisfied (banks, government, customers) · key players (shareholders, CEO, Board) · keep informed (employees, vendors, suppliers, legal experts) · low priority (business magazines, media houses).
Four steps when asked how it is used: identify → assess power and interest → plot on the grid → develop strategies per quadrant.
Stakeholders can suddenly move between quadrants — the GST / Indirect Taxes Department illustration — so re-analyse the grid when the environment changes.

concepts.title: 3.3–3.3.1.1 Strategic Drivers; Industry and Markets
understand: ==**An important aspect of internal analysis is assessing the current performance of the business. And in assessing current performance, the strategic drivers consider what differentiates an organisation from its competitors.**==

The exercise involves analysis of **the key markets in which the organisation operates, its key customers, the products and services it provides, the channels in which those products or services are delivered, and the organisation's competitive advantage**. ==Some of these components are **interlinked**, such as markets and products/services, and channels and key customers in each channel.==

==There can be varied ways to assess current performance and **it is highly subjective based on the management's metrics and ways of doing business** — it can be **profit driven, purpose driven or any other metric** that management sees fit.== But in general, ==**the key strategic drivers of an organisation are four: industry and markets · customers · products/services · channels.**==

**Industry and Markets (§3.3.1).** In terms of the internal environment, ==it is very important for an organisation to **understand its relative position in the industry and in the market in which it operates**==. There are many ways to do this, but all require analysis and understanding of the environment.

==**Similar companies are grouped together into industries. Industry grouping is based on the primary product that a company makes or sells.**== ICAI's illustrations: Maruti, Mahindra, Tata Motors, TVS and Bajaj Auto all sell automotives as their primary product and are categorised into the **automotive industry**; Zara, H&M, Marks & Spencer, Pantaloons, Westside and Uniqlo all sell apparel and accessories for the youth and are categorised under the **apparels industry**.

==**A market is defined as the sum total of all the buyers and sellers in the area or region under consideration.** The value, cost and price of items traded are as per **forces of supply and demand** in a market.== The market may be a **physical entity** or may be **virtual**, like e-commerce websites and applications, and it may be **local or global** depending on which countries the business sells in.

**Is the market the same for all businesses?** ==**No.** Market refers to all the buyers and sellers of a particular product or service, so it would be incorrect to say that the market is the same for all businesses. **Each business has its own set of customers — i.e. its market — and more so, each product within a business has its own market.**== ICAI's illustration: for an FMCG brand selling shampoos, dairy products, flours and washing powder, **each product line has a separate market** to cater to, and therefore strategies specific to the market of concern.

**Analysing industry and markets (§3.3.1.1).** ==Industry and market analysis is extremely important **to identify one's position as compared to the competitors**, who can be of equal size and value, bigger in size and value, or even smaller and newer. **A tool used for this is called Strategic Group Mapping.**==

**Strategic group mapping, as this chapter states it.** A strategic group consists of those rival firms which have **similar competitive approaches and positions in the market**. Companies in the same strategic group can resemble one another in several ways: ==they may have **comparable product-line breadth, sell in the same price/quality range, emphasize the same distribution channels, use essentially the same product attributes to appeal to similar types of buyers, depend on identical technological approaches, or offer buyers similar services and technical assistance**.== ==**An industry contains only one strategic group when all sellers pursue essentially identical strategies and have comparable market positions. At the other extreme, there are as many strategic groups as there are competitors when each rival pursues a distinctively different competitive approach and occupies a substantially different competitive position in the marketplace.**==

The four-step procedure is the same one SM Chapter 2 gives at §2.7.1: identify the differentiating competitive characteristics (price/quality range, geographic coverage, degree of vertical integration, product-line breadth, use of distribution channels, degree of service offered); plot the firms on a two-variable map; assign firms in about the same strategy space to the same strategic group; and draw circles proportional to each group's share of total industry sales revenues.

**ICAI's worked laptop map.** Five companies — ABC, DEF, GHI, XYZ and PQR — sell laptops. The **y-axis is reputation amongst consumers** and the **x-axis is range of products**; reputation is shown both by the **height on the y-axis and the size of the bubble**. Reading it: ==**ABC has few models but great reputation; GHI has a good range and is the most reputed; XYZ and GHI have the same number of models (same x-position) but GHI's reputation is far higher — a bigger bubble, placed higher.**== Strategists can build any number of such scenarios, so the analysis **helps a business understand its competition in terms of two or more factors in a single graphical representation**.

**Where the two chapters meet.** This heading is the one place where the study material itself cross-refers the internal and the external analysis: assessing your *own* relative position (internal) requires mapping *rivals* (external). That is why ICAI's answer to 'write a short note on the key strategic drivers' says of driver 1 that industry and market dynamics are analysed '**often through tools like strategic group mapping**'.
concepts.example: A regional dairy assesses its current performance on four drivers: it is in the packaged-dairy industry (industry), its markets are three states with separate markets for milk, curd and ghee (markets), its customers split into households and institutional buyers (customers), its products range from loose milk to premium ghee (products), and it reaches them through milk booths, kirana stores, modern trade and a delivery app (channels). Mapping rivals on price band against product breadth then shows that nobody sells premium ghee through the app — the position the strategy will take.
keywords: assessing the current performance of the business
what differentiates an organisation from its competitors
industry and markets, customers, products/services, channels
grouping is based on the primary product
sum total of all the buyers and sellers
physical entity or may be virtual
each product within a business has its own market
as many strategic groups as there are competitors

memory.trick: Four drivers = "I-C-P-C" ("Industry, Customers, Products, Channels") — the order ICAI always uses. Remember they are **interlinked in pairs**: markets with products, channels with customers.
key: Industry and markets — relative position; industry by primary product; market = all buyers and sellers
Customers — segmented by needs and spending capacity; customer versus consumer
Products/services — what business are we in; classification, branding, pricing, differentiation
Channels — the distribution system; sales, product and service channels

mistakes: Naming competitive advantage as a fifth driver. The study material lists the firm's competitive advantage among the things the analysis *involves*, but the **key strategic drivers are four**.
Saying the market is the same for all businesses in an industry. ICAI expressly denies it: each business, and each product within a business, has its own market.
Defining an industry by size or ownership. Industry grouping is based on the **primary product** a company makes or sells.
Forgetting that an industry can contain only one strategic group — when all sellers pursue essentially identical strategies — or as many groups as there are competitors.

official_questions.question: Write a short note on the key strategic drivers of an organization.
answer_points: **Strategic drivers are essential elements that influence an organization's ability to differentiate itself from its competitors and achieve competitive advantage. These drivers assess the current performance of the business and provide insights into areas that need focus.**

**1. Industry and Markets:** understanding the industry and markets is crucial for identifying the organisation's relative position. **Industries group similar companies based on their primary products, while markets are defined by the buyers and sellers of these products.** Analysing industry and market dynamics, **often through tools like strategic group mapping**, helps organisations evaluate competition and refine strategies.

**2. Customers:** identifying and understanding customers is a critical driver. **Customers are segmented based on their needs and spending capacity**, which guides product development and marketing strategies. **Differentiating between customers (buyers) and consumers (users) is vital** to tailoring pricing, design and usability strategies effectively.

**3. Products and Services:** products and services are **central to defining the business**. Organisations must assess their offerings, **classify products, and devise strategies for differentiation, branding and pricing**. Product innovation and marketing are key to maintaining competitiveness.

**4. Channels:** the channels through which products and services are delivered **impact on accessibility and customer satisfaction**. Strategies related to **direct, digital or relationship-based marketing** ensure the efficient distribution of offerings to target customers.
**ICAI's closing sentence:** by aligning these drivers with organisational goals, businesses can achieve sustained growth and maintain a competitive edge.
also_asked_as: The identical question with the identical published answer appears as RTP-J26-SQ12, RTP-M26-SQ12, RTP-S25-SQ12, MTP-M26-S1-SQ3a and MTP-S25-S1-SQ3a — six appearances in all, which makes this the most repeated question in SM Chapter 3.

official_questions.question: A consumer technology startup continually revises its business model to align with shifting user behaviour, the rise of new digital platforms and rapid technological advancements. In the context of internal strategic analysis, identify the key internal elements or strategic drivers that the firm is responding to. (5 Marks)
answer_points: The startup is responding to **internal strategic drivers** — the key elements within the organisation that shape its performance and strategic direction. Internal analysis involves assessing these drivers.

**1. Industry and Markets:** the startup closely monitors its relative position in the industry and changing market dynamics; as user behaviour, platforms and technologies evolve, it adapts its model to stay aligned with shifting market expectations.

**2. Customers:** changing user behaviour directly influences customer needs, so the firm must re-segment its customers by needs and spending capacity and re-tailor pricing, design and usability — remembering the distinction between customers who buy and consumers who use.

**3. Products/Services:** the offerings must be reassessed, reclassified and re-differentiated as the technology changes, with branding and pricing strategies revised; product innovation is what keeps the business competitive.

**4. Channels:** the rise of new digital platforms is a change in the channel mix, and the firm must develop or leverage channels that reach its customers — accessibility and customer satisfaction depend on it.
The case is a clean illustration of ICAI's point that the drivers are **interlinked**: the change in technology reaches the firm through all four at once.

concepts.title: 3.3.2–3.3.3 Customers; Product/Services
understand: **Customers (§3.3.2).** ==Understanding the different types of customers to whom the organisation's products or services are sold is **not only important but also the first step in deciding the product/service**. Different customers may have **different needs and require different sales models or distribution channels**.==

ICAI's illustration: for a **headphones brand**, customers can be grouped under **high value, medium value and low value buyers based on the amount they are willing to spend**, which helps the business understand its key customers and focus areas of improvement. The study material even prints the value bands — high value ₹3,500–5,500, medium value ₹1,500–3,500, low value below ₹1,500.

==As customers are often **responsible for the generation of profits** obtained by an organisation, it is important to be able to **collect and display data in order to show customer trends and profitability**. Issues with customers can be identified, and **target areas for growth can be pursued based on the findings**.==

**Customer versus consumer — the distinction ICAI puts in a box.** ==**Consumers are the ones who finally use a product or service, while customers are the buyers of that product. A customer can be a consumer and vice versa.**== But for strategy teams, especially marketing teams, it is important to understand the two separately. ICAI gives two illustrations: a **parent buying stationery** is the customer while the **kids who use it** are the consumers; and **baby diapers** are bought by parents (customers) willing to pay a higher price for higher quality, while the real consumers are the **babies**, who are concerned about comfort and ease — ==**if babies do not accept the product, i.e. if consumers aren't satisfied, it is difficult to retain the buyer, i.e. the customer, as well**==.

==**The pricing-versus-design rule.** From a **pricing** perspective the **customer** is of more importance; from **value creation and design/usability**, the **consumer** needs to be kept at the centre of decision making.== That one sentence is the examinable point of the whole distinction.

**Product/Services (§3.3.3).** Products and services are **closely linked and interrelated with the markets** the organisation wants to serve. In this component the business identifies the key products and services it offers and **how those are performing**, answering the general question: ==**What business are we in and what should be done to win over competition in each product/service we serve?**==

==**Product stands for the combination of 'goods-and-services' that the company offers to the target market.**== Strategies are needed for **managing existing products over time, adding new ones and dropping failed products**; strategic decisions must also be made on **branding, packaging and other product features such as warranties**. Products can be classified as **industrial or consumer, essentials or luxury, durables or perishables**.

Products have a **wide range of quality and workmanship** and these change over time, since **products and markets are infinitely dynamic**; an organisation has to capture such dynamics through a set of policies and strategies. **Some products have consistent customer demand over a long period while others have short life spans.**

**Differentiation and brands.** Products can be differentiated on **size, shape, colour, packaging, brand names, after-sales service** and so on. ==Organisations seek to hammer into customers' minds that their products are different from others. **It does not matter whether the differentiation is real or imaginary. Quite often the differentiation is psychological rather than physical. It is enough if customers are persuaded to believe that the marketer's product is different from others.**== ICAI's illustration: **Head & Shoulders, Olay, Old Spice and Pantene are all produced by the same company, P&G.** Organisations formalise differentiation through **brand names**, generally reinforced with **legal sanctions and protection**; brands let customers identify the product and the organisation behind it, and **customers tend to develop strong brand loyalty** over a period of time.

**Pricing a new product — three objectives.** For a new product, pricing strategies for entering a market must keep at least three objectives in mind: ==**have a customer-centric approach while making a product; produce sufficient returns through a reasonable margin over cost; and increase market share.**==

**The thirteen marketing strategies.** Products and services need heavy investment in reaching out to customers, and over the years a number of marketing strategies have evolved to handle marketing strategically and fight competition:

**(1) Social Marketing** — the design, implementation and control of programs seeking to **increase the acceptability of a social idea, cause or practice** among a target group to bring in social change (ICAI's example: the publicity campaign for prohibition of smoking in Delhi). **(2) Augmented Marketing** — ==**additional customer services and benefits that a product can offer besides the core and actual product**: hi-tech services like **movies on demand, online computer repair services, secretarial services**; such innovative offerings **promise to elevate customer service to unprecedented levels**==. **(3) Direct Marketing** — marketing through advertising media that **interact directly with consumers**, generally calling for a direct response: **catalogue selling, e-mail, telecomputing, electronic marketing, shopping and TV shopping**. **(4) Relationship Marketing** — ==**creating, maintaining and enhancing strong, value-laden relationships with customers and other stakeholders**; ICAI's example is **airlines offering special lounges at major airports for frequent flyers**==.

**(5) Services Marketing** — applying the concepts, tools and techniques of marketing to services, a service being **any activity or benefit that one party can offer to another that is essentially intangible**; it needs different strategies because of **inseparability, variability** and similar characteristics. **(6) Person Marketing** — activities to **create, maintain or change attitudes and behaviour towards a particular person** (politicians, sports stars, film stars). **(7) Organization Marketing** — activities to create, maintain or change attitudes and behaviour of target audiences **towards an organization**; both profit and non-profit organisations practise it. **(8) Place Marketing** — activities directed at attitudes and behaviour **towards particular places** — marketing of business sites, tourism marketing.

**(9) Enlightened Marketing** — ==a marketing philosophy holding that a company's marketing should **support the best long-run performance of the marketing system**, beyond the prevailing mindset; its **five principles** are **customer-oriented marketing, innovative marketing, value marketing, sense-of-mission marketing and societal marketing**==. **(10) Differential Marketing** — a market-coverage strategy in which a firm **targets several market segments and designs separate offers for each** (HUL's Lifebuoy, Lux and Rexona in the popular segment; Dove and Pears in premium). **(11) Synchro-marketing** — ==when demand is **irregular due to season, parts of the day or hour**, causing idle or overworked capacity, synchro-marketing finds ways to **alter the pattern of demand through flexible pricing, promotion and other incentives** (movie tickets priced lower on weekdays)==. **(12) Concentrated Marketing** — a market-coverage strategy in which a firm **goes after a large share of one or few sub-markets**; it can also take the form of **niche marketing**. **(13) Demarketing** — ==marketing strategies **to reduce demand temporarily or permanently**; **the aim is not to destroy demand, but only to reduce or shift it**, used when there is **overfull demand** (overloaded buses in peak hours, over-crowded zoological parks on holidays)==.
concepts.example: A premium headphone brand prices for the customer — the working professional paying ₹4,500 — but designs for the consumer, who may be the same person or their teenage child. It runs differential marketing (three price bands, three sub-brands), augmented marketing (free doorstep replacement), relationship marketing (a loyalty tier), and synchro-marketing (festival discounts to smooth demand). Four of ICAI's thirteen strategies in one product line.

concepts.title: 3.3.4 Channels
understand: ==**Channels are the distribution system by which an organisation distributes its product or provides its service.**==

ICAI's three worked illustrations: **Lakme** sells via retail stores, intermediary stores (Nykaa, Westside, Reliance Trends) and online modes (Amazon, Flipkart, Nykaa online and its own website); **Boat Headphones** sells **only online** via e-commerce platforms like Flipkart and Amazon; **Coca Cola** sells through retail shops across the nation, in each district and town, as well as online via Dunzo, Blinkit and similar.

==**The wider and stronger the channel, the better position a business has to fight and win over competition.** Also, having robust channels of business distribution **helps keep new players away from entering the industry, thus acting as barriers to entry**.==
**The three channels, in the study material's own words:**

==**The sales channel** — these are the **intermediaries involved in selling the product through each channel and ultimately to the end user**. The key question is: **Who needs to sell to whom for your product to be sold to your end user?** ICAI's example: many **fashion designers use agencies** to sell their products to retail organisations so that consumers can access them.==

==**The product channel** — focuses on the **series of intermediaries who physically handle the product on its path from its producer to the end user**. ICAI's example: **Australia Post**, which delivers and distributes many online purchases between seller and purchaser for eBay and other online stores.==

==**The service channel** — refers to the **entities that provide necessary services to support the product, as it moves through the sales channel and after purchase by the end user**. It is an important consideration for **products that are complex in terms of installation or customer assistance**. ICAI's example: a **Bosch dishwasher** may be sold in a Bosch showroom, and once sold it is **installed by a Bosch contracted plumber**.==

==**Why channel analysis matters.** Channel analysis is important **when the business strategy is to scale up and expand beyond the current geographies and markets**. When a business plans to grow to newer markets, they need to **develop or leverage existing channels to get to new customers**. Thus, analysis of channels that suit one's products and customers is **of utmost importance**.==

ICAI's two applications: a **healthcare brand wanting to reach elderly customers** needs to be more focused on the **offline mode**, where agents reach out physically, because most of its potential customers are not active on smartphones; and a **new drink brand acquiring customers** needs to place its products via **every channel possible** — stores and shops alike, plus competitive campaigns to create awareness online through social media.
==**Thus, channels — the partners in growth — play a crucial role in internal strategic alignment.**==

**ICAI's closing box.** 'Ever been to a hill station or a desert or a far-off location on vacation, and still had access to bottled water and cold drinks? This is possible because of **strong channels of distribution**.' The brands it names as having **created competitive advantage in channels**: **Coca Cola, HUL, Patanjali, Asian Paints, Ola.**
concepts.example: A dishwasher maker entering Tier-3 towns maps all three channels: who will sell (a regional distributor plus two online marketplaces — the sales channel), who will physically move the machine (a third-party logistics firm — the product channel), and who will install it and handle complaints (contracted plumbers trained by the company — the service channel). Missing the third is how a complex product fails even when the first two work.

concepts.title: 3.4 Role of Resources and Capabilities: Building Core Competency
understand: ==An organization may be viewed as **an entity endowed with resources and capabilities**. These resources and capabilities may be **so synergized as to impart distinct competencies** that the organization may leverage to its advantage.==

==**C.K. Prahalad and Gary Hamel** have advocated the concept of core competency. They defined core competency as **the collective learning in the organization, especially coordinating diverse production skills and integrating multiple streams of technologies.**== An organization's combination of **technological and managerial know-how, wisdom and experience** are a complex set of capabilities and resources that can lead to a competitive advantage compared to a competitor.

==**Competency is defined as a combination of skills and techniques rather than individual skill or separate technique.** For core competencies it is characteristic to have a combination of skills and techniques which makes the whole organization utilize these several separate individual capabilities. Therefore, **core competencies cannot be built on one capability or single technological know-how; instead it has to be the integration of many resources.**== ==**The optimal way to define core competence is to consider it as the sum of 5 to 15 areas of developed expertise.**==
**The three areas in which major core competencies are identified** (Prahalad and Hamel) — ==**competitor differentiation, customer value, and application to other markets**==:

==**(1) Competitor differentiation.** The company can consider having a core competence **if the competence is unique and it is difficult for competitors to imitate**. This provides an edge compared to competitors and allows the company to provide better products or services **with no fear that competitors can copy it**. The company has to **keep on improving these skills in order to sustain its competitive position**. Competence does not necessarily have to exist within one company to be defined as a core competence: although all companies in the same market would have equal skills and resources, **if one company can perform this significantly better, that company has obtained a core competence**. ICAI's example: it is quite difficult to imitate patented innovation, like **Tesla** winning over competition in electric vehicles.==

==**(2) Customer value.** When purchasing a product or service, it has to **deliver a fundamental benefit for the end customer** in order to be a core competence. It will include **all the skills needed to provide fundamental benefits**. The service or product must have **a real impact on the customer as the reason to choose to purchase**. If a customer has chosen the company without this impact, then the competence is not a core competence and it will not affect the company's market position. **The essence is that the consumer should value the differentiation offered. Without it, the core competency does not make sense.**==

==**(3) Application to other markets.** **Core competence must be applicable to the whole organization; it cannot be only one particular skill or specified area of expertise.** Therefore, although some special capability may be essential or crucial for the success of a business activity, **it will not be considered a core competence if it is not fundamental from the whole organization's point of view**. Thus a core competence is **a unique set of skills and expertise which will be used throughout the organisation to open up potential markets to be exploited**. If the three conditions are met, the company can regard its competence as a core competency.==

**Core competencies in the form of organizational functions.** ICAI's illustration: ==**Marketing and Sales is a core competence of Hindustan Unilever Limited** — HUL has used its resources to form marketing-related capabilities that allow it to market its products in ways superior to competitors, and because of this core competence HUL is capable of **launching new brands in the market successfully**.==

==**A core competency for a firm is whatever it does best.**== ICAI's second illustration: **Wal-Mart focuses on lowering its operating costs**; the cost advantage it has created has allowed the retailer to **price goods lower than most competitors**, and the core competency is derived from the company's **ability to generate large sales volume, allowing it to remain profitable with a low profit margin**.

==**Core competencies are the knowledge, skills and facilities necessary to design and produce core products.** They are **created by superior integration of technological, physical and human resources**. They represent **distinctive skills as well as intangible, invisible, intellectual assets and cultural capabilities**. **Cultural capabilities refer to the ability to manage change, the ability to learn and teamwork.**==

==**Organizations should be viewed as a bundle of a few core competencies, each supported by several individual skills.** **Core-competence-based diversification reduces risk and investment and increases the opportunities for transferring learning and best practice across business units.**==

**Core technological competencies are also corporate assets**, and as assets they **facilitate corporate access to a variety of markets and businesses**. For competitive advantage, a core technological competence should be **difficult for the competitors to imitate**.
ICAI's closing box: **Airtel's marketing campaign about 'Zero Customer Complaints' is about creating a core competency of great customer service.**

Each is small; together they are the 'sum of 5 to 15 areas of developed expertise' ICAI describes — and that is ICAI's own published answer to exactly this question.

concepts.title: 3.4.1 Criteria for Building Core Competencies
understand: ==**Four specific criteria of sustainable competitive advantage that firms can use to determine those capabilities that are core competencies: capabilities that are valuable, rare, costly to imitate, and non-substitutable are core competencies.**==

==**(i) Valuable.** Valuable capabilities are the ones that **allow the firm to exploit opportunities or avert the threats in its external environment**. A firm creates value for customers by effectively using capabilities to exploit opportunities. ICAI's example: **finance companies build a valuable competence in financial services**; and to make such competencies highly successful requires **placing the right people in the right jobs** — **human capital is important in creating value for customers**.==

==**(ii) Rare.** Core competencies are **very rare capabilities and very few of the competitors possess these**. **Capabilities possessed by many rivals are unlikely to be sources of competitive advantage for any one of them.** Competitive advantage results **only when firms develop and exploit valuable capabilities that differ from those shared with competitors**.==

==**(iii) Costly to imitate.** Costly to imitate means **such capabilities that competing firms are unable to develop easily**. ICAI's example: **Intel has enjoyed a first-mover advantage more than once because of its rare fast R&D cycle time capability**, which brought SRAM and DRAM integrated circuit technology and microprocessors to market well ahead of the competitor. **The product could be imitated in due course of time, but it was much more difficult to imitate the R&D cycle time capability.**==

==**(iv) Non-substitutable.** **Capabilities that do not have strategic equivalents are called non-substitutable capabilities.** This final criterion is that **there must be no strategically equivalent valuable resources that are themselves either not rare or imitable.** ICAI's example: for years firms tried to imitate **Tata's low-cost strategy**, but most were unable to duplicate Tata's success — they did not realise that **Tata has a unique culture and attracts some of the top talent in the industry**, and the culture and excellent human capital worked together in implementing the strategy and are the basis for its competitive advantage. **The strategic value of capabilities increases as they become more difficult to substitute.** A second example: competitors are deeply aware of **Apple's operating system (iOS)** success, but **to date no competitor has been able to imitate Apple's capabilities**, which are also **protected through copyrights**.==

==**To sum up: only when a capability is valuable, rare, costly to imitate, and non-substitutable is it a core competence and a source of competitive advantage.** Over time, **core competencies must be supported**. **Core competencies are a source of competitive advantage only when they allow the firm to create value by exploiting opportunities in its external environment.**==

**How ICAI uses the four criteria in a case.** The September 2026 RTP case is instructive. OrthoCare Hospital's robotic knee programme rests on **surgeon expertise, specialised training protocols, coordinated teamwork and a unique organisational culture**; competing hospitals bought the same robotic technology but could not match the outcomes. ICAI's answer names the criterion at work as ==**costly to imitate**==, explaining that such a capability is **created through the superior integration of technological, physical and human resources along with organisational culture, teamwork, experience and accumulated knowledge**, is **developed over time** and **cannot be replicated merely by acquiring similar technology or resources**. That is the template: name the one criterion the facts turn on, then close with all four.

**The three four-item lists, kept apart.** It is worth fixing the difference once: the **four criteria here** (valuable, rare, costly to imitate, non-substitutable) decide **whether a capability is a core competence**. The **four characteristics at §3.6.1** (durability, transferability, imitability, appropriability) decide **how long the resulting advantage lasts and who gets the returns**. The **three areas at §3.4** (competitor differentiation, customer value, application to other markets) decide **where major core competencies are found**. Questions are set on each separately.
concepts.example: Two hospitals buy the same surgical robot. One already has surgeons who have done 2,000 such procedures, a training protocol built over a decade, theatre teams that work as a unit, and a culture that reviews every outcome. Only the second hospital's capability is valuable, rare, costly to imitate and non-substitutable — the robot itself is none of those, because anyone can buy it.

expected_questions.question: Distinguish between the four criteria that determine whether a capability is a core competence and the four characteristics that determine the sustainability of a competitive advantage.
answer_points: **The four criteria (SM §3.4.1)** decide whether a capability *is* a core competence: **valuable** (allows the firm to exploit opportunities or avert threats in its external environment), **rare** (very few competitors possess it, since capabilities shared with many rivals cannot be a source of advantage for any of them), **costly to imitate** (competing firms are unable to develop it easily — Intel's fast R&D cycle time capability) and **non-substitutable** (no strategically equivalent valuable resources that are themselves not rare or imitable — Tata's culture and human capital, Apple's iOS).

**The four characteristics (SM §3.6.1)** decide how long the advantage *lasts* and who gets the returns: **durability** (the rate at which the firm's resources and capabilities deteriorate — product patents become obsolete where innovation is fast, and CEO-dependent capabilities are vulnerable to departure, while consumer brand names can be highly durable), **transferability** (the easier it is to transfer resources and capabilities between companies, the less sustainable the advantage based on them), **imitability** (if they cannot be purchased by a would-be imitator they must be built from scratch — the true test; complexity and corporate culture make imitation difficult) and **appropriability** (the ability of the firm's owners to appropriate the returns on its resource base).
**The practical difference:** the first list is a **qualification test** applied to a capability; the second is a **durability test** applied to an advantage already held.

A third list must not be confused with either: the **three areas** in which major core competencies are identified — competitor differentiation, customer value and application to other markets (Prahalad and Hamel, §3.4).

ICAI's own closing condition joins the two lists: core competencies **must be supported over time**, and they are a source of competitive advantage **only when they allow the firm to create value by exploiting opportunities in its external environment**.
keywords: valuable, rare, costly to imitate, non-substitutable

official_questions.question: Explain the four specific criteria of sustainable competitive advantages that a company can use to determine the capabilities that are core competencies. (5 Marks)
answer_points: Capabilities that are **valuable, rare, costly to imitate, and non-substitutable** are core competencies.

**(i) Valuable:** valuable capabilities are the ones that allow the firm to **exploit opportunities or avert the threats in its external environment**. A firm creates value for customers by effectively using capabilities to exploit opportunities. Finance companies build a valuable competence in financial services; making such competencies highly successful requires **placing the right people in the right jobs**, and human capital is important in creating value for customers.

**(ii) Rare:** core competencies are **very rare capabilities and very few of the competitors possess these**. Capabilities possessed by many rivals are unlikely to be sources of competitive advantage for any one of them; competitive advantage results only when firms develop and exploit **valuable capabilities that differ from those shared with competitors**.

**(iii) Costly to imitate:** such capabilities that **competing firms are unable to develop easily**. Intel has enjoyed a first-mover advantage more than once because of its rare **fast R&D cycle time capability**, which brought SRAM and DRAM integrated circuit technology and microprocessors to market well ahead of the competitor. The product could be imitated in due course, **but it was much more difficult to imitate the R&D cycle time capability**.

**(iv) Non-substitutable:** capabilities that **do not have strategic equivalents**. There must be **no strategically equivalent valuable resources that are themselves either not rare or imitable**. Firms tried for years to imitate Tata's low-cost strategy but could not duplicate its success, because **Tata has a unique culture and attracts some of the top talent in the industry**; the culture and human capital together are the basis of its advantage. No competitor has yet imitated **Apple's iOS capabilities**, which are also protected through copyrights.

**To sum up:** only when a capability is valuable, rare, costly to imitate and non-substitutable is it a core competence and a source of competitive advantage; core competencies must be supported over time, and are a source of advantage **only when they allow the firm to create value by exploiting opportunities in its external environment**.
