concepts.title: 3.5 Combining External and Internal Analysis (SWOT Analysis)
understand: ==**SWOT analysis is the analysis of a business's strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats.** **The primary objective of a SWOT analysis is to help organizations develop a full awareness of all the factors — external as well as internal — involved in making a business decision.**==

==**When to do it.** SWOT analysis **shall be implemented before all company actions**, whether it is **exploring new initiatives, revamping internal policies, considering opportunities to grow or altering a plan midway**. One shall also use SWOT analysis **to discover recommendations and strategies, with a focus on leveraging strengths and opportunities to overcome weaknesses and threats**.==

==Since its creation, SWOT has been **the most widely used tool for business owners to grow their companies**. Sometimes it is wise to perform SWOT analysis just **to check on the current landscape** of the business to improve operations as needed. **The analysis can show areas where an organization is performing well, as well as areas that need improvement.**==

**The 2×2 frame.** The study material prints SWOT as a grid of **origin against effect**: **internal origin (attributes of the organization)** versus **external origin (attributes of the environment)**, crossed with **helpful to achieving the objective** versus **harmful to achieving the objective**. So **strengths** = internal and helpful; **weaknesses** = internal and harmful; **opportunities** = external and helpful; **threats** = external and harmful.

**ICAI's worked example — a law firm.** **Strengths:** multiple partners with varied expertise; long-term contractual service agreements; 70 years of brand value; services spread across 20 states of India; 400+ employee strength to deliver work. **Weaknesses:** run by old methods; no automation of work and documentation; not very employee-friendly culture. **Opportunities:** automation-driven advancement; start-ups can be supported with experienced partners; investment in technology can multiply returns. **Threats:** online players entering the market; AI-based solutions and applications; price point of online being very competitive; speed of work becoming faster by the day.

==**The benefit and the criticism.** **The benefit of this analysis is that it identifies the complex issues for an organisation and puts them into a simple framework.** **On the other hand, one of the major criticisms of this tool is that it does not generally provide for evaluation of strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats in the competitive context.**== Therefore an organisation using SWOT **should consider relative competitors and the external factors affecting the organisation**. ==**Although a simple tool, it is a useful starting point for analysis.**==

==**Internal or external? ICAI answers its own question.** 'Internal analysis is more focused on understanding the existing structure and competencies of the business, thus highlighting the Strengths and Weaknesses, while External Analysis is about identifying and preparing for uncontrollables which can either be Opportunities or threats. **Therefore, SWOT Analysis is a tool which is used for both Internal and External Analysis.**' This is why the heading is called 'Combining External and Internal Analysis' and why it sits in the internal-environment chapter.==

**What a full-mark SWOT case answer looks like.** ICAI's published case answers do not theorise: they print a **four-cell grid filled from the facts in the stem**. In the GreenGardens answer the strengths cell reads 'high-quality, pesticide-free produce' and the weaknesses cell 'limited distribution channels' — words taken straight from the question. Then they add a line of strategy: leverage the strengths against the opportunities to overcome the weaknesses and threats.

That is the criticism the study material names: SWOT puts complex issues into a simple frame but does not weigh them against what rivals are doing, so the firm must add the competitive context itself.

expected_questions.question: Write a short note on SWOT analysis, covering its meaning, the four terms, its benefit and its major criticism.
answer_points: **SWOT analysis is a tool used by organizations for evolving strategic options for the future.** The term refers to the analysis of **strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats** facing a company. **Strengths and weaknesses are identified in the internal environment, whereas opportunities and threats are located in the external environment.**

**Strength** is an **inherent capability of the organization which it can use to gain strategic advantage over its competitor**. **Weakness** is an **inherent limitation or constraint of the organisation which creates a strategic disadvantage** to it.

**Opportunity** is a **favourable condition in the external environment which enables it to strengthen its position**. **Threat** is an **unfavourable condition in the external environment which causes a risk for, or damage to, the organisation's position**.

**The major purpose** of SWOT analysis is to enable the management to **create a firm-specific business model that will best align, fit or match organisational resources and capabilities to the demands of the environment** in which it operates.

**Benefit:** it **identifies the complex issues for an organisation and puts them into a simple framework**. **Criticism:** it **does not generally provide for evaluation of strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats in the competitive context**, so the organisation should also consider relative competitors and the external factors affecting it. Although a simple tool, **it is a useful starting point for analysis**.

answer_points: The primary objective of SWOT analysis is to help organisations develop a **full awareness of all the factors — internal as well as external — involved in making a business decision**. It is therefore necessary to conduct SWOT analysis before strategy formulation, for the following reasons.

**It identifies the Strengths and Weaknesses (internal factors) and Opportunities and Threats (external factors).** This ensures that **management considers all aspects before deciding on a strategic move**.

**It helps in discovering recommendations and strategies**, with a focus on **leveraging strengths and opportunities while working to overcome weaknesses and threats**. This lays the base for realistic and practical strategies.
**SWOT highlights both the areas where the business is performing well and the areas which need improvement.** This helps organisations **align resources efficiently** to achieve objectives.
**Periodic SWOT analysis helps organisations check the current landscape** of their business and make necessary improvements in operations, **keeping strategies relevant to changing circumstances**.

**It places complex internal and external issues into a simple framework**, making it easier for managers to identify challenges and opportunities — though the organisation must add the competitive context, which SWOT does not itself supply.

concepts.title: 3.6–3.6.1 Competitive Advantage; Sustainability of Competitive Advantage
understand: **The questions ICAI opens the heading with.** Why do some companies succeed while others fail? Why did **Hindustan Motors** do so well for several decades? How did **Apple** return from near obsolescence in the late 1990s to become the world leader and a dominant technology company? In the Indian airline industry, how has **Indigo Airlines** managed to keep increasing its revenues and profits through both good times and bad, while rivals struggled? ==**For most, if not all, companies, achieving superior performance relative to rivals is the ultimate challenge. If a company's strategies result in superior performance, it is said to have a competitive advantage.**==

==Strategic management involves the **development of competencies that managers can use to achieve better performance and a competitive advantage**. **Competitive advantage allows a firm to gain an edge over rivals when competing.** It is **'a set of unique features of a company and its products that are perceived by the target market as significant and superior to the competition.'**==

==**In other words, an organization is said to have competitive advantage if its profitability is higher than the average profitability for all companies in its industry.**== ICAI prints Jack Welch alongside: **"If you don't have a competitive advantage, don't compete."**

==**The competitive advantage is the achieved advantage over rivals when a company's profitability is greater than the average profitability of firms in its industry. It is achieved when the firm successfully formulates and implements the value creation strategy and other firms are unable to duplicate it or find it too costly to imitate.** Further, **a firm is successful in achieving competitive advantage only after other firms' efforts to duplicate or imitate it fail.**==

**Sustainability of competitive advantage (§3.6.1).** ==**The sustainability of competitive advantage, and a firm's ability to earn profits from it, depends upon four major characteristics of resources and capabilities: durability, transferability, imitability and appropriability.**==

==**(i) Durability.** The period over which a competitive advantage is sustained **depends in part on the rate at which a firm's resources and capabilities deteriorate**. **In industries where the rate of product innovation is fast, product patents are quite likely to become obsolete.** Similarly, **capabilities which are the result of the management expertise of the CEO are also vulnerable to his or her retirement or departure.** On the other hand, **many consumer brand names have a highly durable appeal.**==

==**(ii) Transferability.** Even if the resources and capabilities on which an advantage is based are durable, **it is likely to be eroded by competition from rivals**. The ability of rivals to attack a position of competitive advantage **relies on their gaining access to the necessary resources and capabilities**. **The easier it is to transfer resources and capabilities between companies, the less sustainable will be the competitive advantage which is based on them.**==

==**(iii) Imitability.** **If resources and capabilities cannot be purchased by a would-be imitator, then they must be built from scratch. How easily and quickly can the competitors build the resources and capabilities on which a firm's competitive advantage is based? This is the true test of imitability.** ICAI's example: **in financial services, innovations lack legal protection and are easily copied.** Here again **the complexity of many organizational capabilities can provide a degree of competitive defense**: **where capabilities require networks of organizational routines, whose effectiveness depends on the corporate culture, imitation is difficult.**==

==**(iv) Appropriability.** **Appropriability refers to the ability of the firm's owners to appropriate the returns on its resource base.** Even where resources and capabilities are capable of offering sustainable advantage, **there is an issue as to who receives the returns on these resources**. This means that **rewards are directed to from where the funds were invested, rather than creating an advantage with no actual reward to people who invested capital.**==

**How ICAI words the same four in a past paper.** The May 2025 answer re-words them usefully: **durability** is 'how long the firm's resources and capabilities remain effective before they deteriorate or become obsolete' — patents date fast in technology, while strong brand names are highly durable; **transferability** 'determines how easily a competitor can acquire or replicate the resources and capabilities', for instance **by hiring key personnel or acquiring technology** — the harder access is, the more sustainable the advantage; **imitability** asks how easily competitors can imitate or develop the same resources, and is harder where imitation requires **complex processes, organizational routines or a firm's unique corporate culture**; **appropriability** is the ability of the firm's owners to appropriate the returns, raising the question of **who receives the returns** on resources capable of offering sustainable advantage.

**Reading the two lists together.** §3.4.1's four criteria (valuable, rare, costly to imitate, non-substitutable) ask whether a capability **qualifies** as a core competence. §3.6.1's four characteristics ask whether the advantage it produces will **last** and whether the firm's owners will **keep the returns**. Note that 'imitability' appears in both, from opposite sides: costly to imitate is a qualification, and low imitability is what sustains.

expected_questions.question: Define competitive advantage as the study material does, and state when a firm can be said to have achieved it.
answer_points: For most, if not all, companies, **achieving superior performance relative to rivals is the ultimate challenge**; if a company's strategies result in superior performance, it is said to have a competitive advantage.

**Competitive advantage allows a firm to gain an edge over rivals when competing.** It is **'a set of unique features of a company and its products that are perceived by the target market as significant and superior to the competition.'**

**The profitability test:** an organisation is said to have competitive advantage **if its profitability is higher than the average profitability for all companies in its industry**. ICAI prints Jack Welch's line alongside — 'If you don't have a competitive advantage, don't compete.'

**When it is achieved:** competitive advantage is the achieved advantage over rivals when a company's profitability is greater than the industry average. **It is achieved when the firm successfully formulates and implements the value creation strategy and other firms are unable to duplicate it or find it too costly to imitate.**

**The final condition:** a firm is successful in achieving competitive advantage **only after other firms' efforts to duplicate or imitate it fail**. Strategic management therefore involves developing the competencies managers can use to achieve better performance and that advantage.
keywords: significant and superior to the competition
only after other firm's efforts… fail

official_questions.question: In order to get better performance and sustainable competitive advantages, a company has to focus on the characteristics of its resources and capabilities. In view of this, explain the major characteristics of resources and capabilities. (5 Marks)
answer_points: To achieve better performance and sustainable competitive advantage, a company must focus on the **four major characteristics of its resources and capabilities which determine the sustainability of its competitive advantage**.

**(i) Durability:** how long the firm's resources and capabilities **remain effective before they deteriorate or become obsolete**. For example, in industries with rapid product innovation such as technology, **patents may quickly become outdated**; in contrast, **strong brand names often possess a high degree of durability**, contributing to sustained competitive advantage.

**(ii) Transferability:** how easily a competitor can **acquire or replicate** the resources and capabilities. If key resources and capabilities can be easily transferred between firms — **through hiring key personnel or acquiring technology** — the competitive advantage is less sustainable. **The more difficult it is for rivals to gain access to similar resources, the more sustainable the advantage.**

**(iii) Imitability:** how easily competitors can **imitate or develop the same resources and capabilities**. If imitation requires **complex processes, organizational routines or is dependent on a firm's unique corporate culture, it becomes difficult to replicate**. For instance, in financial services, where innovations are not legally protected, **imitation is easier, reducing sustainability**.

**(iv) Appropriability:** the ability of the **firm's owners to appropriate the returns on its resource base**. Even where resources and capabilities are capable of offering sustainable advantage, **there is an issue as to who receives the returns** on these resources.
Taken together, the four decide not only whether an advantage survives but who keeps the profit it generates.
keywords: hiring key personnel or acquiring technology

concepts.title: 3.6.2 Michael Porter's Generic Strategies (with the Best-Cost Provider Strategy)
understand: ==**According to Porter, strategies allow organizations to gain competitive advantage from three different bases: cost leadership, differentiation, and focus. Porter called these base generic strategies.**== They are termed generic ==**because they can be pursued by any type or size of business firm and even by not-for-profit organisations**==. **This opening sentence appears in every ICAI answer on this heading — write it first.**

==**Cost leadership** emphasizes on **producing standardized products at a very low per-unit cost for consumers who are price-sensitive**. **Differentiation** is a strategy aimed at **producing products and services considered unique industry-wide and directed at consumers who are relatively price-insensitive**. **Focus** means **producing products and services that fulfil the needs of small groups of consumers with very specific taste**.==

Porter's strategies imply **different organizational arrangements, control procedures and incentive systems**. ==**Larger firms with greater access to resources typically compete on a cost leadership and/or differentiation basis, whereas smaller firms often compete on a focus basis.**==

**The 2×2 that generates four of the five.** The figure crosses **competitive scope** (broad target / narrow target) with **competitive advantage** (low-cost products or services / differentiated products or services): broad + low cost = **Cost Leadership**; broad + differentiated = **Differentiation**; narrow + low cost = **Focused Cost Leadership**; narrow + differentiated = **Focused Differentiation**.

Porter stresses **cost-benefit analysis to evaluate 'sharing opportunities' among existing and potential business units** — ==**sharing activities and resources enhances competitive advantage by lowering costs or raising differentiation**== — and the need for firms to **'transfer' skills and expertise among autonomous business units** effectively.

**COST LEADERSHIP (§3.6.2.1).** ==It is a **low-cost competitive strategy that aims at a broad mass market**. It requires **vigorous pursuit of cost reduction in the areas of procurement, production, storage and distribution** of the product or service, **and also economies in overhead costs**. Because of its lower costs the cost leader **is able to charge a lower price than most competitors and still earn satisfactory profits**.== ICAI's examples: **McDonald's** fast-food restaurants, and **Decathlon Group's** mega sports stores.

A primary reason for pursuing **forward, backward and horizontal integration** is to gain cost-leadership benefits. ==**Generally, cost leadership must be pursued in conjunction with differentiation.**== Cost elements affecting the choice include **economies or diseconomies of scale, learning and experience curve effects, the percentage of capacity utilization achieved, and linkages with suppliers and distributors**, plus **the potential for sharing costs and knowledge within the organization, R&D costs, labour costs, tax rates, energy costs and shipping costs**. ==**This internal strategy of sharing resources to build a competitive advantage is called synergy benefit.**==

==**Cost leadership is especially effective when the market is composed of many price-sensitive buyers, and when there are few ways to achieve product differentiation**== — and further, when **buyers do not care much about differences from brand to brand**, or when there are **a large number of buyers with significant bargaining power**. ==**The basic idea is to underprice competitors and thereby gain market share, driving some of the competitors out of the market.**==

==A successful cost leadership strategy **usually permeates the entire firm**, as evidenced by **high efficiency, low overheads, limited perks, intolerance of waste, intensive screening of budget requests, wide span of controls, rewards linked to cost containment, and broad employee participation in cost control efforts**.==

**Risks of cost leadership:** competitors may **imitate the strategy, driving overall industry profits down**; **technological breakthroughs** in the industry may make the strategy ineffective; or **buyer interests may swing to other differentiating features besides price**.

**Achieving cost leadership — six actions.** (1) **Prompt forecasting of demand** of a product or service. (2) **Optimum utilization of the resources** to achieve cost advantages. (3) **Achieving economies of scale**, thus lower per-unit cost. (4) **Standardisation of products for mass production** to yield lower cost per unit (McDonald's). (5) **Invest in cost-saving technologies** and use advanced technology for smart efficient working. (6) **Resistance to differentiation till it becomes essential.**

**Advantages of cost leadership, force by force.** **Rivalry** — competitors are likely to avoid a price war, since the low-cost firm will continue to earn profits even after competitors compete away their profits. **Buyers** — powerful buyers cannot exploit the cost leader and will continue to buy its product. **Suppliers** — cost leaders can **absorb greater price increases from suppliers** before they need to raise prices for customers. **Entrants** — low-cost leaders **create barriers to market entry** through continuous focus on efficiency and cost reduction. **Substitutes** — low-cost leaders are more likely to **lower costs to induce existing customers to stay, invest in developing substitutes, and even purchase patents**.

**Disadvantages of cost leadership.** (1) **Cost advantage may not last long as competitors may imitate cost reduction techniques.** (2) **Cost leadership can succeed only if the firm can achieve higher sales volume.** (3) Cost leaders tend to keep costs low by **minimizing cost of advertising, market research, and research and development, but this approach can prove to be expensive in the long run**. (4) **Technological advancement is a great threat to cost leaders.**

**DIFFERENTIATION (§3.6.2.2).** ==Aimed at a **broad mass market**, it involves **the creation of a product or service that is perceived by the customers as unique**. The uniqueness can be associated with **product design, brand image, features, technology, dealer network or customer service**. Because of differentiation, **the business can charge a premium for its product**.== ICAI's example: **Domino's Pizza** offering home delivery within 30 minutes or the order is free.

==**Differentiation does not guarantee competitive advantage**, especially if standard products sufficiently meet customer needs or if rapid imitation by competitors is possible. **Durable products protected by barriers to quick imitation by competitors are better.**== Successful differentiation can mean **greater product flexibility, greater compatibility, lower costs, improved service, less maintenance, greater convenience or more features**. Differentiation **should be pursued only after a careful study of buyers' needs and preferences** to determine the feasibility of incorporating one or more differentiating features into a unique product. A successful differentiation strategy allows a firm **to charge a higher price and to gain customer loyalty**, because consumers may become strongly attached to the differentiated features. Special features can include **superior service, spare parts availability, engineering design, product performance, useful life, gas mileage, or ease of use**.

**Risks of differentiation:** the unique product **may not be valued high enough by customers to justify the higher price** — when that happens, **a cost leadership strategy will easily defeat a differentiation strategy**; and competitors may **develop ways to copy the differentiating features quickly**, so firms must find **durable sources of uniqueness that cannot be imitated quickly or cheaply**. ICAI's example of a durable source: **Amazon Prime's two-hour delivery**.

==**The three bases of differentiation.** **Product** — innovative products that meet customer needs can be an area of advantage; the pursuit of a new product offering can be costly in R&D, production and marketing, but the payoff can be great as customers flock to be among the first (Apple iPhone). **Pricing** — price fluctuates with supply and demand and may be influenced by the customer's ideal value; companies can **either offer the lowest price or attempt to establish superiority through higher prices** (Apple iPhone charging higher prices). **Organisation** — **maximizing the power of a brand or using the specific advantages an organization possesses**; **location advantage, name recognition and customer loyalty** can all differentiate (Apple's 'fanboys/fangirls').==

**Achieving differentiation — six strategies.** (1) **Offer utility to the customers and match products with their tastes and preferences.** (2) **Elevate or improve performance of the product.** (3) **Offer high-quality product or service for buyer satisfaction.** (4) **Rapid product innovation** to keep up with a dynamic environment. (5) Taking steps for **enhancing brand image and brand value**. (6) **Fixing product prices based on the unique features of the product and the buying capacity of the customer.**

**Advantages of differentiation, force by force.** **Rivalry** — **brand loyalty acts as a safeguard**; customers will be less sensitive to price increases as long as their needs are satisfied. **Buyers** — they **do not negotiate for price** as they get special features and have fewer options. **Suppliers** — because differentiators charge a premium, they can **afford to absorb higher costs of supplies**. **Entrants** — innovative features are an expensive offer, so new entrants generally avoid them. **Substitutes** — substitute products **cannot replace differentiated products which have high brand value and enjoy customer loyalty**.

**Disadvantages of differentiation.** (1) **In the long term, uniqueness is difficult to sustain.** (2) **Charging too high a price for differentiated features may cause the customer to switch off to another alternative** — ICAI's example is the shift of iPhone users to other Android flagship phones. (3) **Differentiation fails to work if its basis is something that is not valued by the customers** — home delivery of packed snacks in 30 minutes would not even be a differentiator.

**FOCUS STRATEGIES (§3.6.2.3).** ==A successful focus strategy **depends on an industry segment that is of sufficient size, has good growth potential, and is not crucial to the success of other major competitors**.== Strategies such as **market penetration and market development** offer substantial focusing advantages. ==**Midsize and large firms can effectively pursue focus-based strategies only in conjunction with differentiation or cost leadership-based strategies.** All firms in essence follow a differentiated strategy, because **only one firm can differentiate itself with the lowest cost**, so the remaining firms must find other ways to differentiate.==

==**Focus strategies are most effective when consumers have distinctive preferences or requirements, and when rival firms are not attempting to specialize in the same target segment.** **Risks:** numerous competitors recognising the successful focus strategy and imitating it, or consumer preferences drifting towards the product attributes desired by the market as a whole.== An organisation using a focus strategy may concentrate on **a particular group of customers, geographic markets, or particular product-line segments** in order to **serve a well-defined but narrow market better than competitors who serve a broader market** (Ferrari sports cars).

==**Focused cost leadership** requires **competing based on price to target a narrow market**. A firm following this strategy **does not necessarily charge the lowest prices in the industry; instead it charges low prices relative to other firms that compete within the target market.**== ==**Focused differentiation** requires **offering unique features that fulfil the demands of a narrow market**. Narrow markets are defined differently in different settings: some firms concentrate on **a particular sales channel, such as selling over the internet only**; others target **particular demographic groups** (Rolls-Royce selling a limited number of high-end, custom-built cars).==

**Achieving a focused strategy — four actions.** (1) **Selecting specific niches which are not covered by cost leaders and differentiators.** (2) **Creating superior skills for catering to such niche markets.** (3) **Generating high efficiencies for serving such niche markets.** (4) **Developing innovative ways in managing the value chain.**

**Advantages of focus.** (1) **Premium prices can be charged** for the focused product or service. (2) **Due to tremendous expertise in the goods and services offered, rivals and new entrants may find it difficult to compete.** **Disadvantages of focus.** (1) **Firms lacking in distinctive competencies may not be able to pursue focus strategy.** (2) **Due to the limited demand of the product or service, costs are high, which can cause problems.** (3) **In the long run the niche could disappear or be taken over by larger competitors by acquiring the same distinctive competencies.**

**BEST-COST PROVIDER STRATEGY (§3.6.2.4).** ==**The new model of best-cost provider strategy is a further development of the above three generic strategies. It is directed towards giving customers more value for the money by emphasizing on both low cost and upscale differences. The objective is to keep costs and prices lower than those of other sellers of "comparable products".**== It can be done through ==**(a) offering products at a lower price than what is being offered by rivals for products with comparable quality and features, OR (b) charging a similar price as the rivals for products with much higher quality and better features**==. ICAI's example: **android flagship phones from OnePlus, Xiaomi, Oppo and Vivo**, all giving better quality at the lowest prices to penetrate the market.

**The five generic competitive strategies, named.** ICAI's second figure lists them as: **Overall Low-Cost Leadership Strategy · Broad Differentiation Strategy · Best-Cost Provider Strategy · Focused Low-Cost Strategy · Focused Differentiation Strategy**, with the best-cost provider sitting in the middle of the grid between lower cost and differentiation, serving a broad cross-section of buyers.
concepts.example: Four firms in one market. A quick-service chain standardises its menu for mass volume and underprices rivals — cost leadership. A premium pizza brand promises delivery in 30 minutes or free — differentiation. A maker of hand-built sports cars serves a tiny segment at a premium — focused differentiation. A phone brand matches flagship features at a mid-range price — best-cost provider. Only the fourth is trying to do two things at once, which is why ICAI calls it 'a further development' of the other three.

memory.trick: Five strategies on one grid: **broad** × (low cost / differentiated) gives **Cost Leadership / Differentiation**; **narrow** × (low cost / differentiated) gives **Focused Cost Leadership / Focused Differentiation**; and the **Best-Cost Provider** sits in the middle, doing both for a broad cross-section.

More value for money — lower price for comparable quality, or same price for higher quality (OnePlus, Xiaomi)

mistakes: Writing 'focus' without specifying **focused cost leadership** or **focused differentiation**. ICAI's cases turn on which.

Calling affordability-plus-premium-features 'differentiation'. When a case says a product **balances affordability with premium features**, or gives **comparable quality at a lower price**, the answer is the **best-cost provider strategy** — ICAI's published answer to the ARP Motors case.

Giving cost leadership's conditions as its advantages. The **conditions** are many price-sensitive buyers and few ways to differentiate; the **advantages** are stated force by force against rivalry, buyers, suppliers, entrants and substitutes.

Forgetting that cost leadership 'must generally be pursued in conjunction with differentiation', and that midsize and large firms can pursue focus **only in conjunction with** differentiation or cost leadership.
Listing only two bases of differentiation. There are **three**: product, pricing and organisation — and pricing can mean either the lowest price *or* a deliberately higher one.

expected_questions.question: State the four actions by which a focused strategy is achieved, and the advantages and disadvantages of pursuing one.
answer_points: **Achieving a focused strategy:** (1) **selecting specific niches which are not covered by cost leaders and differentiators**; (2) **creating superior skills for catering to such niche markets**; (3) **generating high efficiencies for serving such niche markets**; (4) **developing innovative ways in managing the value chain**.

**Advantages:** **premium prices can be charged** by organisations for their focused products or services; and **due to the tremendous expertise in the goods and services offered, rivals and new entrants may find it difficult to compete**.

official_questions.question: In a business strategy, consider a firm pursuing cost leadership to become the lowest-cost producer in its industry. For this approach to be effective, what key conditions must be present? However, cost leadership is not without its risks — state them. (5 Marks)
answer_points: **Cost Leadership Strategy aims at becoming the lowest-cost producer in an industry while offering products or services of acceptable quality.** It enables the firm to **charge lower prices than competitors and still earn satisfactory profits**.

**Key conditions.** Striving to be a low-cost producer can especially be effective **when the market is composed of many price-sensitive buyers** and **when there are few ways to achieve product differentiation**.
**Risk 1:** the **cost advantage may not last long as competitors may imitate cost reduction techniques**.
**Risk 2:** **cost leadership can succeed only if the firm can achieve higher sales volume.**

**Risk 3:** cost leaders tend to keep their costs low by **minimizing cost of advertising, market research, and research and development, but this approach can prove to be expensive in the long run**. **Risk 4:** **technological advancement is a great threat to cost leaders.**

**ICAI's closing sentence:** while cost leadership can provide a strong competitive advantage, its success depends on **favourable conditions and continuous vigilance to avoid risks that may undermine its effectiveness**.
keywords: few ways to achieve product differentiation

official_questions.question: Explain differentiation strategy as one of the generic strategies by Michael Porter. What are the major bases of differentiation? Also outline the strategies which can help achieve the differentiation strategy. (1 + 2 + 2 = 5 Marks)
answer_points: **Differentiation strategy** focuses on **offering unique products or services to a broad market**, allowing firms to **stand out from competitors and charge premium prices**. Uniqueness can stem from **design, features, technology or service**.
**Basis 1 — Product:** innovative or new products that cater to customer needs can give a competitive edge; though expensive in terms of R&D and marketing, they attract customers.
**Basis 2 — Pricing:** pricing can be used as a differentiator — **either through low prices or premium pricing backed by product superiority**.
**Basis 3 — Organisation:** organisational advantages like **brand strength, location or customer loyalty** can be used for differentiation.

**Strategies to achieve differentiation:** (1) **offer utility to customers and match products with their tastes and preferences**; (2) **elevate product performance**; (3) **provide high-quality products or services to ensure buyer satisfaction**; (4) **engage in rapid product innovation to meet changing demands**; (5) **enhance brand image and brand value**; (6) **fix product prices considering product uniqueness and customers' buying capacity**.
Note ICAI's own mark split — 1 for the meaning, 2 for the three bases, 2 for the six strategies — and allocate writing time the same way.

official_questions.question: Pearl India Ltd. is a major packaged food company which dominates in some sectors like snacks, dairy, biscuits and instant meals. It offers high quality and unique products that match the taste and preference of the customers. It always takes steps to enhance brand image and charge a premium price for which buyers do not negotiate. Often the unique features of their products that are not available with their competitors help them to gain competitive advantage. Identify and explain Michael Porter's generic strategy being followed by Pearl India Ltd. What are the disadvantages of following such strategy? (1 + 1 + 3 = 5 Marks)
answer_points: Pearl India Ltd. is following the **Differentiation Strategy** propounded by Michael Porter. Differentiation strategy is **aimed at a broad market and involves the creation of products or services that are perceived by customers as unique**. The uniqueness may be associated with **product quality, features, brand image, technology or customer preferences**. Because of differentiation, **the business can charge a premium price and gain competitive advantage**.

**Application to the facts:** Pearl India Ltd. offers **high quality and unique food products matching customer tastes and preferences**. It continuously **enhances its brand image and charges premium prices for which buyers do not negotiate**. The **special features of its products help it gain a strong competitive position over rivals**.
**Disadvantage 1:** **in the long run, uniqueness may be difficult to sustain as competitors may imitate product features.**
**Disadvantage 2:** **charging very high prices for differentiated products may force customers to switch to alternative products.**
**Disadvantage 3:** **differentiation strategy fails if the basis of differentiation is not valued by customers.**

official_questions.question: ARP Motors, an automobile company, was struggling in the competitive SUV market in India. As a business strategist, you recommended that ARP launch a compact SUV that balances affordability with premium features. Identify and explain the strategy recommended. (5 Marks)
answer_points: The strategy recommended is the **Best-Cost Provider Strategy**.

The best-cost provider strategy is **directed towards giving customers more value for their money by emphasizing both low cost and premium features**. The objective is to **keep costs and prices lower than those of other sellers of comparable products while offering better quality and superior features**.

**Application:** a compact SUV that balances affordability with premium features is precisely the combination — ARP is neither the cheapest nor the most differentiated, but offers more value for the money than rivals selling comparable products.

**The two routes available to ARP:** offer the vehicle **at a lower price than rivals for comparable quality and features**, or **charge a similar price as rivals for a vehicle of much higher quality and better features**.

**Why not the other four:** cost leadership would require standardised products at the lowest per-unit cost for price-sensitive buyers; differentiation would require uniqueness industry-wide for price-insensitive buyers; the focused variants would require a narrow target segment. A compact SUV for the mass Indian market with premium features fits none of those and all of the best-cost provider's definition.
ICAI's own illustration of the strategy is the android flagship segment — OnePlus, Xiaomi, Oppo and Vivo giving better quality at the lowest prices.

official_questions.question: ABC Ltd. is a beverage manufacturing company. It chiefly manufactures soft drinks. The products are priced on the lower side, which has made the company a leader in the business, holding 35 percent of the market share. The R&D of the company developed a formula for manufacturing sugar-free beverages; on successful trial and approval the company was granted permission to manufacture them. This company is the pioneer to launch sugar-free beverages, which are sold at a relatively higher price and have been accepted widely by a class of customers, proving profitable. Identify the strategy employed by ABC Ltd. and mention what measures could be adopted to achieve the employed strategy.
answer_points: **According to Porter, strategies allow organizations to gain competitive advantage from three different bases: cost leadership, differentiation, and focus. Porter called these base generic strategies.**

**ABC Ltd. has opted for the Differentiation Strategy.** The company has **invested a huge amount in R&D and developed a formula for manufacturing sugar-free beverages to give the customer value and quality**. They are **pioneers and serve specific customer needs that are not met by other companies in the industry**. The new product has been accepted by a class of customers.
**Differentiated and unique sugar-free beverages enable ABC Ltd. to charge relatively higher for its products, hence making higher profits and maintaining its competitive position in the market.**

**Measures to achieve differentiation:** offer **utility to customers and match products with their tastes and preferences**; **elevate or improve performance of the product**; offer **high-quality products for buyer satisfaction**; pursue **rapid product innovation** to keep up with a dynamic environment; take steps for **enhancing brand image and brand value**; and **fix product prices based on the unique features of the product and the buying capacity of the customer**.

Note the examiner's design: the stem mentions low prices and market leadership first, which tempts 'cost leadership'. The question asks about the strategy employed **for the new product**, which is differentiation — a reminder to read which part of the business the question is about.
keywords: specific customer needs that are not met

official_questions.question: EliteWheels Ltd. is a luxury automobile manufacturer that caters to affluent customers seeking exclusivity and high-end features. The company offers premium vehicles with cutting-edge technology, customization options and top-tier customer service. Unlike mass-market car brands, EliteWheels charges a significant premium, ensuring that only a niche segment of customers can afford them. It also invests heavily in advanced engineering and innovation to maintain its superior quality and brand prestige. Identify and explain the strategy adopted by EliteWheels Ltd.
answer_points: According to Michael Porter, competitive advantage can be derived from **three generic strategies: cost leadership, differentiation, and focus**.

EliteWheels Ltd. **targets a niche market segment** by offering unique and high-value automobiles tailored to the needs of affluent consumers. While the company **manages its costs efficiently, it does not compromise on the quality or exclusivity of its products**.
By maintaining **superior craftsmanship, advanced technology and high personalization levels, the brand commands a premium price** for its vehicles.
**Thus the strategy adopted by EliteWheels Ltd. is Focused Differentiation.**

**A focused differentiation strategy involves offering distinctive features that cater to a specific market segment.** Companies employing this strategy may target **a specific customer demographic, geographic region, or sales channel**. **Firms that compete based on uniqueness and focus on a specialized market segment follow a Focused Differentiation Strategy.**
The discriminator against plain differentiation is the word **niche**: differentiation aims at a broad mass market, focused differentiation at a narrow one.
keywords: specific customer demographic, geographic region, or sales channel
also_asked_as: RTP-S26-SQ13 sets the same pattern for Elite Motors Ltd. serving ultra-high-net-worth individuals with hand-stitched leather interiors and bespoke design, and ICAI's answer again names Focused Differentiation — adding that the objective is to satisfy the specific needs of a niche market by providing superior quality, exclusivity, innovation or customised features for which customers are willing to pay a premium. Note that ICAI prints that question under its own 'Chapter 4' heading although the concept is this one. MTP-M24-S2-SQ4b reaches the same answer for StarTech Solutions, an aerospace firm serving unique high-end clients, and adds the advantage of strong customer loyalty from catering to a specific niche.

official_questions.question: Despite high commodity inflation, shortage of components and the threat of a third wave of the COVID-19 pandemic, manufacturers of packaged goods, home appliances and consumer electronics expect business to grow by 12 to 25 percent. A leading company in home appliances, XXP India, is planning to launch various innovative product designs and offer loyalty programmes to lure consumers. With reference to Michael Porter's generic strategies, identify which strategy XXP India has planned for. Explain how this strategy will be advantageous to the company to remain profitable.
answer_points: **According to Michael Porter, strategies allow organizations to gain competitive advantage from three different bases: cost leadership, differentiation, and focus. Porter called these base generic strategies.**

XXP India has planned a **Differentiation Strategy**: **innovative product designs** create a product perceived as unique, and **loyalty programmes** build the customer attachment that differentiation depends on.

**Advantages, force by force.** **Rivalry** — brand loyalty acts as a safeguard against competitors, and customers become less sensitive to price increases as long as their needs are satisfied. **Buyers** — they do not negotiate for price, as they get special features and have fewer options in the market.

**Suppliers** — because differentiators charge a premium price, they can afford to **absorb higher costs of supplies**, which matters directly in a period of high commodity inflation and component shortage.

**Entrants** — innovative features are an expensive offer, so new entrants generally avoid them because it is tough to provide the same product with special features at a comparable price. **Substitutes** — substitute products cannot replace differentiated products which have high brand value and enjoy customer loyalty.
The case rewards linking the advantages to the stem's own pressures: inflation and shortages are exactly what a premium price lets the firm absorb.
keywords: brand loyalty acts as a safeguard

official_questions.question: EcoTrend, a growing e-commerce company, competes with industry giants by offering premium, eco-friendly products at high prices, targeting environmentally conscious consumers. Meanwhile, its competitor, BudgetBazaar, focuses on offering the widest range of products at the lowest prices to the mass market. Identify the generic strategies of both. (5 Marks)
answer_points: **Michael Porter's Generic Strategies framework includes Cost Leadership, Differentiation and Focus Strategies.**

**EcoTrend — Differentiation Focus Strategy:** it **targets a niche market** (environmentally conscious consumers) with **premium, eco-friendly products**, and gains a competitive advantage **through product uniqueness and sustainability**.

**BudgetBazaar — Cost Leadership:** the **widest range at the lowest prices to the mass market** is the signature of a low-cost competitive strategy aimed at a broad mass market, serving many price-sensitive buyers.
The pairing is instructive because the two firms sit in **different cells of the same grid**: EcoTrend is narrow-target and differentiated; BudgetBazaar is broad-target and low-cost.

For EcoTrend the risks are those of focus — the niche could disappear or be taken over by larger competitors acquiring the same distinctive competencies — while for BudgetBazaar they are those of cost leadership: imitation of cost-reduction techniques, dependence on high sales volume, and technological advancement.
keywords: widest range at the lowest prices

mcqs.question: Mukul faced intense competition in an undifferentiated industry. To address this, he opted for a cost-cutting strategy to attract customers. Which generic strategy is he pursuing?

options.A: Differentiation
options.B: Focused differentiation
options.C: Cost leadership
options.D: Best-cost provider

mcqs.explanation: Cost leadership is especially effective 'when the market is composed of many price-sensitive buyers and when there are few ways to achieve product differentiation' (SM §3.6.2.1) — an undifferentiated industry is precisely that. ICAI key: (c).

why_wrong.A: The industry is undifferentiated, so uniqueness is not available.
why_wrong.B: No narrow target segment is described.
why_wrong.D: Best-cost provider needs upscale differences as well as low cost.

mcqs.trap: 'Cost-cutting' is an action; the strategy it serves is cost leadership, whose published condition the stem quotes almost word for word.

mcqs.question: While implementing a cost leadership strategy, Horizon Technologies went beyond just streamlining their production processes. What other factors did they consider to achieve cost efficiencies?

options.A: Only advertising and market research budgets
options.B: Only the price charged to customers
options.C: Procurement, storage and distribution, together with economies in overhead costs and linkages with suppliers and distributors
options.D: Only the number of employees

mcqs.explanation: Cost leadership 'requires vigorous pursuit of cost reduction in the areas of procurement, production, storage and distribution of product or service and also economies in overhead costs', with cost elements including linkages with suppliers and distributors (SM §3.6.2.1). ICAI key: (c).

why_wrong.A: Minimising advertising and research is a *consequence* the study material warns can be expensive in the long run.
why_wrong.B: Price is the output of the cost position, not a source of cost efficiency.
why_wrong.D: Headcount alone is far narrower than the published list.

mcqs.trap: Option A is a real feature of cost leaders but is listed among its disadvantages, not among the areas of cost reduction.

mcqs.question: EcoForge's strategy of appealing to environmentally conscious builders and developers by emphasizing its eco-friendly materials is an example of which type of generic strategy by Michael Porter?

options.A: Cost leadership
options.B: Differentiation
options.C: Focused cost leadership
options.D: Best-cost provider

mcqs.explanation: Creating a product perceived by customers as unique — here, eco-friendly materials for buyers who value them — and directing it at relatively price-insensitive consumers is differentiation (SM §3.6.2.2). ICAI key: (b).

why_wrong.A: No standardised low-cost mass production is described.
why_wrong.C: No low-price narrow-market play is described.
why_wrong.D: No claim of comparable quality at a lower price is made.

mcqs.trap: 'Environmentally conscious builders' sounds like a niche, which tempts focused differentiation; the stem describes an industry-wide appeal on an attribute, which is plain differentiation.

mcqs.question: Why did Zing's differentiation strategy fall short in the market?

options.A: Because it failed to standardise its products
options.B: Because it did not target a narrow enough segment
options.C: Because the differentiating features were not valued highly enough by customers to justify the higher price
options.D: Because it did not invest in advertising

mcqs.explanation: SM §3.6.2.2 names exactly this risk: 'the unique product may not be valued high enough by customers to justify the higher price. When this happens, a cost leadership strategy will easily defeat a differentiation strategy.' ICAI key: (c).

why_wrong.A: Standardisation belongs to cost leadership.
why_wrong.B: Narrowing the target would make it a focus strategy, not fix the differentiation.
why_wrong.D: Advertising is not the published failure mode.

mcqs.trap: The published risk is about the *customer's valuation*, not the firm's execution.

mcqs.question: What type of strategy did Café Delight use to differentiate itself from competitors in the Indian restaurant industry?

options.A: Cost leadership through standardised menus
options.B: Differentiation through a unique blend of Australian and Indian culinary experiences
options.C: Focused cost leadership in a single city
options.D: Demarketing to manage overfull demand

mcqs.explanation: A product perceived by customers as unique — here a culinary blend no rival offers — is differentiation, whose uniqueness may be associated with product design, brand image, features or service (SM §3.6.2.2). ICAI key: (b).

why_wrong.A: The case describes uniqueness, not standardisation.
why_wrong.C: The chain expanded across cities; no low-price narrow play is described.
why_wrong.D: Demarketing is a marketing technique from §3.3.3, not a generic strategy.

mcqs.trap: Option D is a real term from the same chapter dropped into a strategy question.

mcqs.question: How does Titan Tech's use of Michael Porter's differentiation strategy help it stay competitive?

options.A: By offering the lowest-priced products in every segment
options.B: By narrowing its market to a single demographic group
options.C: By creating offerings customers perceive as unique, which supports a premium price and builds customer loyalty that acts as a safeguard against rivalry
options.D: By matching rivals' prices for comparable quality

mcqs.explanation: Differentiation allows a firm to charge a higher price and gain customer loyalty, and brand loyalty acts as a safeguard against competitors while making customers less price-sensitive (SM §3.6.2.2). ICAI key: (c).

why_wrong.A: That is cost leadership.
why_wrong.B: That would be focused differentiation.
why_wrong.D: That is the best-cost provider strategy.

mcqs.trap: Each distractor is the correct description of a different one of the five strategies.

mcqs.question: How does ZGE's best-cost provider strategy benefit its healthcare SBU?

options.A: By offering the lowest-priced services in the market
options.B: By maintaining high service quality at competitive prices
options.C: By targeting only premium customers in developed markets
options.D: By focusing solely on cost-cutting measures

mcqs.explanation: The best-cost provider strategy gives customers more value for the money by emphasising both low cost and upscale differences, keeping costs and prices lower than other sellers of comparable products (SM §3.6.2.4). The case's telemedicine service costs 30% less without compromising quality. ICAI key: (b).

why_wrong.A: That would be cost leadership; the best-cost provider is not necessarily cheapest.
why_wrong.C: Premium-only targeting would be differentiation or focused differentiation.
why_wrong.D: Pure cost-cutting abandons the 'upscale differences' half of the strategy.

mcqs.trap: Options A and D are the two halves of cost leadership; the best-cost provider must hold quality and cost together.

mcqs.question: MedTech Solutions' focus on developing affordable telemedicine platforms and AI-driven diagnostic tools reflects which of Porter's generic strategies?

options.A: Overall cost leadership for a broad mass market
options.B: Focused cost leadership in a single geography
options.C: Best-cost provider — more value for the money, combining affordability with advanced features
options.D: Demarketing of excess demand

mcqs.explanation: Affordability combined with advanced technology is the best-cost provider's definition: more value for the money by emphasising both low cost and upscale differences (SM §3.6.2.4). ICAI key: (c).

why_wrong.A: Cost leadership requires standardised products at the lowest per-unit cost, not advanced AI features.
why_wrong.B: No single narrow geography is described.
why_wrong.D: Not a generic strategy.

mcqs.trap: 'Affordable' alone suggests cost leadership; paired with 'AI-driven' it is the best-cost provider.

mcqs.question: ValueMart is a discount retail chain that targets budget-conscious consumers by offering a wide range of products at the lowest prices. Which generic strategy is ValueMart following?

options.A: Differentiation
options.B: Focused differentiation
options.C: Cost leadership
options.D: Best-cost provider

mcqs.explanation: A low-cost competitive strategy aimed at a broad mass market of price-sensitive buyers, underpricing competitors to gain market share, is cost leadership (SM §3.6.2.1). ICAI key: (c).

why_wrong.A: No uniqueness is claimed.
why_wrong.B: The target is broad, not narrow.
why_wrong.D: No upscale differences are offered alongside the low price.

mcqs.trap: 'Wide range' might suggest differentiation through breadth; the stem's decisive words are 'budget-conscious' and 'lowest prices'.

mcqs.question: Nav-Uday's core business model of offering reliable, functional scooters at an affordable price prior to market disruption was best described as:

options.A: Cost leadership aimed at a broad mass market of price-sensitive buyers
options.B: Focused differentiation for a niche of premium buyers
options.C: Best-cost provider with upscale features
options.D: Differentiation on brand image

mcqs.explanation: Reliable, functional products at an affordable price for a broad market is the low-cost competitive strategy aimed at a broad mass market — standardised products at a low per-unit cost for price-sensitive consumers (SM §3.6.2.1). ICAI key: (a).

why_wrong.B: No niche or premium positioning is described.
why_wrong.C: 'Functional' is the opposite of upscale differences.
why_wrong.D: No uniqueness of brand image is claimed.

mcqs.trap: 'Reliable' sounds like a differentiator; paired with 'functional' and 'affordable' it describes acceptable quality at low cost.

mcqs.question: A firm competes on price within a narrow target market but does **not** charge the lowest prices in the industry — only low prices relative to other firms competing in that same segment. This is:

options.A: Overall cost leadership
options.B: Focused cost leadership
options.C: Best-cost provider
options.D: Focused differentiation

mcqs.explanation: SM §3.6.2.3: 'A focused cost leadership strategy requires competing based on price to target a narrow market. A firm that follows this strategy does not necessarily charge the lowest prices in the industry. Instead, it charges low prices relative to other firms that compete within the target market.'

why_wrong.A: Overall cost leadership aims at a broad mass market and underprices the industry.
why_wrong.C: The best-cost provider adds upscale differences and serves a broad cross-section.
why_wrong.D: Focused differentiation competes on uniqueness, not price.

mcqs.trap: The distinctive clause — low prices *relative to the target market*, not the industry — is exactly what the question tests.

mcqs.question: The internal strategy of sharing resources within an organisation to build a competitive advantage is called, in the study material:

options.A: Synergy benefit
options.B: Experience effect
options.C: Appropriability
options.D: Vertical integration

mcqs.explanation: SM §3.6.2.1: 'This internal strategy of sharing resources to build a competitive advantage is called synergy benefit.' Porter stresses cost-benefit analysis of sharing opportunities among existing and potential business units, since sharing activities and resources enhances advantage by lowering costs or raising differentiation.

why_wrong.B: The experience effect is the fall in unit costs with cumulative volume.
why_wrong.C: Appropriability is who receives the returns on the resource base.
why_wrong.D: Vertical integration is a growth strategy, though pursued partly for cost-leadership benefits.

mcqs.trap: All four are genuine terms from Paper 6B; only one is attached to resource sharing.

mcqs.question: As per the study material, midsize and large firms can effectively pursue focus-based strategies:

options.A: Only if they abandon all broad-market activity
options.B: Only in conjunction with differentiation or cost leadership-based strategies
options.C: Only in markets with no existing competitors
options.D: Only by acquiring smaller niche players

mcqs.explanation: SM §3.6.2.3: 'Midsize and large firms can effectively pursue focus-based strategies only in conjunction with differentiation or cost leadership-based strategies.' Smaller firms, by contrast, often compete on a focus basis alone.

why_wrong.A: No such requirement is stated.
why_wrong.C: The stated condition is that rivals are not specialising in the same target segment, not that there are none.
why_wrong.D: Acquisition is how the niche may be *taken over* — a disadvantage of focus, not a requirement.

mcqs.trap: Option D inverts a disadvantage into a prescription.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is named in the study material as a **risk of pursuing a focus strategy**?

options.A: That buyers will not negotiate on price
options.B: That suppliers will absorb cost increases
options.C: That brand loyalty will make customers price-insensitive
options.D: That numerous competitors may recognise the successful focus strategy and imitate it, or that consumer preferences may drift towards the attributes desired by the market as a whole

mcqs.explanation: SM §3.6.2.3 states both risks in exactly these terms. The other options are *advantages* of differentiation stated force by force.

why_wrong.A: An advantage of differentiation against buyers.
why_wrong.B: An advantage of differentiation against suppliers.
why_wrong.C: An advantage of differentiation against rivalry.

mcqs.trap: Three options are genuine quotations from the neighbouring heading, attached to the wrong strategy and the wrong column.

recap: Open every answer with: Porter's three bases — cost leadership, differentiation, focus — called generic because any type or size of firm, even not-for-profits, can pursue them.

Cost leadership: standardised products, lowest per-unit cost, broad mass market, price-sensitive buyers; effective when there are many price-sensitive buyers and few ways to differentiate; six achieving actions; four disadvantages.
Differentiation: unique industry-wide, price-insensitive buyers, premium price; three bases (product, pricing, organisation); six achieving strategies; three disadvantages.

Focus: a segment of sufficient size, good growth potential, not crucial to major competitors; focused cost leadership competes on relative price, focused differentiation on uniqueness; large firms need it in conjunction with another strategy.
Best-cost provider: more value for the money — lower price for comparable quality, or the same price for much higher quality (OnePlus, Xiaomi).
Five generic strategies in all: overall low-cost leadership, broad differentiation, best-cost provider, focused low-cost, focused differentiation.
